articles.summary: The prosecution camp of the House of Representatives has decided to forgo its plan to let former senator Antonio Trillanes IV take the witness stand in the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President…

blocks.text: October 2, 2026 | 12:00am

Lead prosecutor Rep. Gerville Luistro manifested before the Senate impeachment court their consensus to do away with Trillanes’ scheduled testimony and to present witnesses from seven banks, several insurance firms and the Anti-Money Laundering Council next week.
AFP / Noel Celis

MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution camp of the House of Representatives has decided to forgo its plan to let former senator Antonio Trillanes IV take the witness stand in the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
“We seek the kind indulgence of the honorable impeachment court for the belated final position on this particular concern,” Luistro said.

Trillanes, an arch critic of the family of detained former president Rodrigo Duterte, was supposed to take the witness stand shortly after Davao Mayor Sebastian Duterte did, as prosecutors tried to establish and prove that the Vice President committed conflict of interest in her business dealings while in political office.
On social media, Trillanes said he requested the House prosecution panel to withdraw him as witness, adding that he would present his evidence in a press briefing instead.
“I have many new and serious pieces of evidence against Sara. Let the senator-judges and the people decide whether these are significant or not,” he added.

Sen. Raffy Tulfo criticized the prosecution for being “palpak” (sloppy) in its presentation of some witnesses, such as in Monday’s hearing when the panel presented a police firearms official and trying to link his testimony to Duterte’s alleged hidden wealth.
Without naming anyone, Tulfo chided the prosecution for fielding a public prosecutor who acted “cute” during the direct examination. – Mark Ernest Villeza, Marc Jayson Cayabyab

articles.title: SC settles quorum question on Senate shakeup
articles.summary: The Supreme Court dismissed two petitions challenging the Senate’s decision to convene on June 3 with just a quorum of 12 members – a session that ousted Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano as…

blocks.text: October 2, 2026 | 12:00am
In a notice posted by Sen. Francis Pangilinan on his social media accounts yesterday, the high court junked the petitions filed by lawyers Valeriano Loon and Zigfred Diaz questioning the session.
The STAR / Jesse Bustos

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court dismissed two petitions challenging the Senate’s decision to convene on June 3 with just a quorum of 12 members – a session that ousted Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano as Senate president and installing Sen. Sherwin Gatchalian as Senate president pro tempore.

The notice said the Court ruled that the petitioners failed to show that the Senate acted with grave abuse of discretion when the Gatchalian bloc launched an 11th-hour coup with the help of Sen. Francis Escudero to end two days of deadlock.
The SC ruled that the June 3 session “appear to be in accord with the facts and applicable law and jurisprudence” – contradicting what Cayetano’s allies had been branding as illegal.
Voting threshold

Malacañang respects the Supreme Court’s ruling to dismiss three petitions seeking to reverse the Senate impeachment court on the two-thirds voting threshold issue to decide the fate of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Domingo Cayosa, former national president of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines, told “Storycon” on One News yesterday that the SC is subtly staying out of the political fray.

“One message is the Senate already knows what to do, because on technicalities alone, the justices have not cleared the petitions,” Cayosa said. – Ghio Ong, Alexis Romero, Bella Cariaso, Mark Ernest Villeza, Marc Jayson Cayabyab

articles.title: Defense: Properties mentioned were in Sara’s SALN
articles.summary: The properties mentioned by the prosecution witnesses before the Senate impeachment court yesterday were included in the statement of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN) of Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: October 2, 2026 | 12:00am
“That is our position, your honor,” defense counsel Lindon Miguel Bacquel said.
Philstar.com illustration

MANILA, Philippines — The properties mentioned by the prosecution witnesses before the Senate impeachment court yesterday were included in the statement of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN) of Vice President Sara Duterte, according to the defense team.

The prosecution presented Register of Deeds officers Kathy Florence Baldonado from Davao City and Marco Pineda from the Island Garden City of Samal, Davao del Norte, who both testified on two pieces of land in Davao City and Samal Island, amounting to P6 million and P3.45 million, respectively.
The prosecution said Duterte failed to declare the two properties in her SALN and accused her of unexplained wealth, false SALNs and continued business interests.
Bacquel said the testimonies of Baldonado and Pineda were “irrelevant” as the prosecution drilled down on the alleged unexplained wealth of Duterte.
Presentation of AMLC

The defense team has moved to postpone the prosecution’s presentation of the witness from the Anti-Money Laundering Council, saying they should be given time to study the documents submitted by the AMLC before the impeachment court.
In her manifestation, defense lead counsel Sheila Sison noted that they only received the email at 11:28 a.m. yesterday.

The AMLC is expected to present to the Senate impeachment court its report on the P6.7 billion in transactions linked to the bank accounts of Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio under Article II of the impeachment on unexplained wealth.
Sison added that the defense team needed to review at least 23 to 24 boxes of documents.

articles.title: DOJ ‘almost ready to file’ extradition petition on Quiboloy
articles.summary: The Department of Justice is “almost ready to file the petition” on the request of the United States government to send embattled pastor Apollo Quiboloy who is facing multiple charges of…

blocks.text: October 2, 2026 | 12:00am

Kingdom of Jesus Christ Pastor Apollo Quiboloy faces senators for the first time during the public hearing of the Committee on Women, Children, Family Relations and Gender Equality Wednesday, October 23, 2024.
Senate Public Relations and Information Bureau

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Justice (DOJ) is “almost ready to file the petition” on the request of the United States government to send embattled pastor Apollo Quiboloy who is facing multiple charges of trafficking and cash smuggling.
“We’re in the final stages already of vetting, we are just doing legal scrubbing,” Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida said in a media briefing yesterday.
He added the agency was “almost ready to file the petition.”

He also noted the agency was “now governed by the Supreme Court rules on extradition,” wherein he said “there is a clear provision on the right of the person to be extradited and it would undergo a process.”

When asked for a timeline for the filing of the extradition petition, Vida said that there were “several factors including defenses of the Quiboloy camp and the decision of the authority handling the petition, all beyond our control.”

The Supreme Court’s Rules on Extradition Proceedings, specifically A. M. No. 22-03-29-SC, contains a provision on the “temporary surrender” of the person facing extradition to be decided by the local court handling his pending case under Section 17, Rule 2.

“Where the judgment granting Extradition cannot be enforced because of Extraditee’s pending criminal cases in the Philippines, the Central Authority may file a motion in the court where the said criminal case requesting the temporary surrender of the Extraditee to the Requesting State,” read a part of the provision.
The Central Authority referred to the justice secretary or “any of the designated and authorized State Counsels.”
The provision also stated, “The said court may allow the temporary surrender, under such conditions as it deems as proper considering the circumstances of the case.”

The US government in July this year transmitted its extradition request for Quiboloy, founder of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ religious group who faces charges of sexual trafficking and bulk cash smuggling.
Aside from the lawsuit in the US, human trafficking and child sexual abuse cases were also pressed against Quiboloy before courts in Pasig City and Quezon City.

articles.title: Palace: P46 billlion aid ready for ‘Super El Niño’ ,
articles.summary: The government has allocated more than P46 billion this year to respond to the impact of “Super El Niño,” Malacañang said yesterday, as it urged the public not to panic…

blocks.text: October 2, 2026 | 12:00am

Bernard Alan Racoma, director of the Education Division of the UP Institute of Environmental Science and Meteorology points to the position of El Niño at the Project NOAH office in UP Diliman yesterday
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The government has allocated more than P46 billion this year to respond to the impact of “Super El Niño,” Malacañang said yesterday, as it urged the public not to panic because efforts are underway to help sectors hit by the weather phenomenon.

Palace press officer Claire Castro said P6.2 billion is ready for release to the agriculture department to provide farmers and fisherfolk with fuel assistance, fertilizer and other farm inputs. The Marcos administration also set aside P39.82 billion to support disaster management efforts.

The Marcos administration is proposing to increase the NDRRM Fund to P45.67 billion in next year’s national budget. Of the amount, P14.67 billion is allocated for local government disaster rehabilitation and reconstruction.
The proposed budget for 2027 also contains P9.885 billion in Quick Response Funds for frontline agencies, with a mechanism for additional funding support from the NDRRM Fund when needed.

To enhance food-security buffers, the administration is seeking an P11.18 billion outlay for the National Food Authority’s rice buffer stocking next year. It is also proposing a P4.5-billion budget for crop insurance covering some 2.34 million small farmers and fisherfolk and P46.356-billion outlay for the National Irrigation Administration, including P30.437 billion for irrigation restoration and development.

The agriculture department has also proposed the expansion of the minimum access volume for corn to 500,000 metric tons as it braces for the possible impact of the El Niño on the supply of the staple.
Castro also advised the public not to panic, noting that the Philippines had managed to address the impact of the weather phenomenon.
No water interruption yet
Consumers may not experience water interruptions yet amid the looming “very strong” El Niño this month, the National Water Resource Board (NWRB) said.
In an interview with dzBB, NWRB executive director Sevillo David Jr. said the dams have replenished enough water so far with the rains brought by several tropical cyclones in August and the habagat.

articles.title: PCG drives away Chinese research vessel off Batanes
articles.summary: A Chinese research vessel retreated from the waters of Itbayat, Batanes yesterday after “sustained pressure” from the Philippine Coast Guard.

blocks.text: October 2, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — A Chinese research vessel retreated from the waters of Itbayat, Batanes yesterday after “sustained pressure” from the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG).

According to PCG spokesman for the West Philippine Sea Rear Adm. Jay Tarriela, BRP Teresa Magbanua approached Jia Hai Ke 7 and launched a rigid-hull inflatable boat to disrupt the research vessel’s “illegal marine scientific research” activity in the area.
The PCG also deployed an aircraft from Basco Airport to support the Teresa Magbanua in driving away the research ship.

Tarriela said the research ship made evasive maneuver as the Teresa Magbanua continued issuing radio challenges. A China Coast Guard vessel with bow number CCG-2503 arrived in the area and issued its own radio challenge, Tarriela said.

“A government law enforcement ship moving to shield a supposedly private research vessel conducting illegal MSR in another country’s exclusive economic zone raises serious questions about who Jia Hai Ke 7 is really working for,” the PCG official said.
The PCG confirmed the presence of Jia Hai Ke 7 about 37 nautical miles northwest of Itbayat, Batanes using a dark vessel detection on Sept. 28.
Authorities said the research ship used a spoofing tool for its automatic identification system as it registered its location in Papua New Guinea just 20 hours after it set sail from China.

“Jia Hai Ke 7 has held its position in the same waters for four days, which is a clear indication that it is conducting MSR,” said Tarriela, stressing that the Department of Foreign Affairs has not given its consent to the Chinese vessel’s research activity.
Tarriela also raised concerns over the data the vessel may have collected from undersea cable corridors in the Luzon Strait, which, he stressed, are part of the country’s critical infrastructure.
The PCG said the research vessel left its position at 11:42 a.m., moving away from Itbayat, Batanes at 4.6 knots.
Tarriela said the Teresa Magbanua will continue to shadow Jia Hai Ke 7 until it exits the country’s exclusive economic zone.
Amid the latest Chinese’ maritime incursion, the Philippines rejected Beijing’s call for Manila to stop raising the sea dispute and the arbitral ruling, at the 81st UN General Assembly.
Exercising its right to reply to China’s call, the Philippines said its “legal position is well established” under UNCLOS and the 2016 arbitral ruling.
Sun Lei, China’s deputy permanent representative to the UN, raised the call earlier before the UN.

“There is no legal basis for China’s expansive maritime claims, including claims based on historic rights, and that the freedom of navigation, overflight, and other lawful uses of the sea under UNCLOS must be respected,” Manila said.

States oppose coercive or destabilizing conduct, including the use of coast guard, military, or maritime militia forces to harass or obstruct lawful operations and the parties should abide by the award and resolve disputes peacefully in accordance with international law.
The Philippines also rejected any suggestion that its lawful exercise of sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction constitutes provocation.

“The Philippines remains concerned by actions at sea that interfere with the exercise of its rights and jurisdiction in its maritime zones and that create risks to Philippine vessels and personnel,” Manila said.
Security meetings

Meanwhile, Finland’s Ambassador Saija Nurminen paid a courtesy visit on Wednesday to Armed Forces of the Philippines chief Gen. Antonio Nafarrete and discussed strengthening bilateral defense and security cooperation.
Also on Wednesday, the Philippines and Sweden held high-level discussions aimed at further enhancing cooperation between the two countries.

The Department of National Defense (DND) and Sweden’s defense ministry convened for the 3rd Philippines–Sweden Joint Committee Meeting on Logistics and Defense Industry Cooperation in Mandaluyong City.

“The Joint Committee Meeting reaffirmed the shared commitment of the Philippines and Sweden to sustaining dialogue, enhancing interoperability, and promoting mutually beneficial defense cooperation founded on mutual respect, shared interests, and adherence to international law,” DND spokesman Arsenio Andolong said.

He said the meeting reaffirmed “both countries’ commitment to deepening bilateral defense cooperation and exploring practical areas of collaboration in support of regional peace, stability, and defense resilience.” – Pia Lee-Brago, Michael Punongbayan

articles.title: AMLC freezes assets linked to flood mess
articles.summary: The Anti-Money Laundering Council has secured another court order freezing more than 100 financial accounts and other assets linked to a lawmaker and several individuals and entities allegedly…

blocks.text: October 2, 2026 | 12:00am
A photo of the Court of Appeals in Ermita, Manila.
The STAR, File

MNILA, Philippines — The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) has secured another court order freezing more than 100 financial accounts and other assets linked to a lawmaker and several individuals and entities allegedly involved in corruption, plunder and flood control project anomalies.
The Court of Appeals (CA) issued the freeze order on Sept. 21 after finding probable cause that the assets were related to plunder under Republic Act 7080, according to the AMLC.
A freeze order temporarily prevents covered assets from being withdrawn, transferred or disposed of while authorities investigate their possible links to unlawful activities.
The order covers 86 bank accounts, four investment accounts, one insurance policy and 25 virtual asset wallets, or digital accounts used to hold and transfer virtual assets such as cryptocurrencies.

According to the AMLC, the use of multiple recipients and financial channels made the funds harder to trace and increased their transactional distance from their alleged source. The council said the transactions were traced to funds allegedly linked to corruption and plunder cases involving the lawmaker.
The AMLC did not identify the lawmaker, the company or the other parties covered by the order.
In an earlier response to The STAR, the council said it is legally barred from disclosing information that could reveal the identities of persons or entities covered by freeze order proceedings.
The latest case also highlights the increasing use of newer financial channels in transactions involving suspected illicit funds.
The AMLC said funds in the case passed through virtual asset service providers and multiple virtual asset wallets, adding layers that made their movement more difficult to trace.

“The AMLC will continue working closely with partner agencies and financial service providers to identify, trace, restrain and recover suspected illicit assets, while preventing the misuse of both traditional and emerging financial channels for corruption, money laundering,” it said.

articles.title: Government ready to answer petitions vs BSKE postponement
articles.summary: The Marcos administration is prepared to justify President Marcos’ decision to sign into law the measure postponing the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) originally slated for…

blocks.text: October 2, 2026 | 12:00am
Palace press officer Claire Castro said the Senate and the Commission on Elections are now coordinating with the Office of the Solicitor General, for their next move.
STAR / Ernie Penaredondo

MANILA, Philippines — The Marcos administration is prepared to justify President Marcos’ decision to sign into law the measure postponing the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) originally slated for next month, to 2028, Malacañang said yesterday.

“But they are ready to respond immediately and follow the order of the Supreme Court once they receive a copy of the petition. Within five days from receipt of the said petition, they will comply,” Castro said in a briefing.
Castro said Marcos and the lawmakers believe that postponing the barangay and youth council polls is the right thing to do.
“The Office of the Solicitor General will fight for the stance of the executive (branch), Comelec and the Senate,” the undersecretary added.
The postponement of the BSKE is contained in Republic Act 12326, which fixed the term of office of village and youth council officials to five years.

The measure, signed into law last Sept. 24, permitted incumbent officers to remain in their posts for two additional years. The new law states that no elective barangay official shall serve for more than two consecutive terms in the same position and no elective youth council official shall serve for more than one term in the same post.

With the extension of their terms by two years, incumbent elective barangay officials will be regarded as having completed one term in their respective positions. Incumbent officials serving their last term in the same post can no longer run for the same position in the November 2028 BSKE.

Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal earlier filed a petition questioning the legality of the law, saying it violates the electorate’s right to vote by postponing the 2026 BSKE under the guise of fixing the officials’ term of office. He argued that the law effectively allows incumbent barangay and SK officials to “hold over” their positions for three years or from December 2025 to November 2028.
The Supreme Court has directed the respondents, including the Office of the President, to comment on the petition.

articles.title: Eala makes TIME Risin Stars list
articles.summary: The world has taken notice of tennis ace Alex Eala, who has made inroads in the sport and captured the imagination of the Philippine diaspora.

blocks.text: October 2, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — The world has taken notice of tennis ace Alex Eala, who has made inroads in the sport and captured the imagination of the Philippine diaspora.
TIME magazine has named the 21-year-old phenom one of the world’s most influential rising stars, alongside the likes of Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar and British singer-songwriter Raye.

The magazine selected 100 people for its annual TIME100 Next list who “seem to have come out of nowhere, somehow magicking themselves into the culture, seizing the zeitgeist, or leapfrogging their industries with little advance notice,” according to editor-in-chief Sam Jacobs. The magazine has been publishing the list since 2019.
Tennis legend Rafael Nadal penned the tribute to his protégé, saying that he was “lucky enough” to have followed Eala’s career from her time as a student at the Rafa Nadal Academy in Manacor, Spain.

“One of her greatest strengths is precisely her ability to listen, learn and keep improving,” Nadal said of Eala. “But perhaps more importantly, Alex remains a wonderful person—warm, approachable and humble.”
“It isn’t easy to handle becoming a true phenomenon at such a young age,” Nadal went on, “and she deserves a lot of credit for keeping her feet on the ground.”
Tennis officials have noticed that Eala has drawn crowds from the Filipino diaspora ever since moving up the WTA rankings.
Canadian Open tournament director Alex Hale told sports outlet The Athletic that her sold-out opening match in August was “really unheard of” since it was on a Wednesday.
Despite reaching a career-high ranking of world No. 18 and winning a WTA 500 title at the Mubadala DC Open, Eala “still has plenty of room to grow,” Nadal believes.
“Now, all that remains is to keep enjoying watching her progress,” he said.

articles.title: Ex-VP aide needs more time after NBI subpoena
articles.summary: he National Bureau of Investigation has summoned Jeffrey Tupas, who reportedly served as information officer of Davao City when Vice President Sara Duterte was mayor, as part of its investigation…

blocks.text: October 2, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has summoned Jeffrey Tupas, who reportedly served as information officer of Davao City when Vice President Sara Duterte was mayor, as part of its investigation into alleged plunder, graft and money laundering.
NBI Director Melvin Matibag signed the subpoena dated Sept. 28 directing Tupas to appear at the NBI headquarters in Pasay City at 10 a.m. yesterday.

The subpoena orders Tupas to provide information and give evidence in connection with the bureau’s investigation into alleged violations of Republic Act 7080, or the Anti-Plunder Act; RA 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act; and RA 9160, or the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001.

The NBI has summoned Tupas after Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. – a dismissed policeman and security officer of former speaker Lord Allan Velasco – claimed that he delivered suitcases containing cash amounting to P2 billion to the Vice President. Gracioso said that the money was delivered to the Dutertes upon instructions from Velasco.

Gracioso said the first time he delivered money to Duterte, then amounting to P20 million, was in 2018 when she was still Davao City mayor. He claimed Duterte instructed him to give the suitcase to a member of her staff, a certain Jeff Tupas.
Response

In a letter received by the Office of NBI Director on Oct. 1, 10:15 a.m., Tupas’ counsel Caesar Europa said the subpoena issued by Matibag was received at the residence of Tupas’ parents in Kabacan, Cotabato in the afternoon of Sept. 29.

“Nonetheless, in relation to the subpoena for Mr. Tupas to appear before you at 10 a.m. on Oct. 1, 2026, the notice is too short for him to comply, particularly considering he is based in Mindanao,” Europa added.
Tupas was involved in a controversy in 2021 after the party he attended was later raided by authorities over suspected illegal drug activity.

“While the scope of what he is supposed to be asked about ‘to provide relevant information on the investigation being conducted by this bureau…’ is a bit wide, it is unreasonable for Mr. Tupas to believe that the inquiry is in relation to the allegations of a certain P/Cpl. Rodulfo M. Gracioso, whose interview and sworn statement are making their rounds in news and social media,” Europa added.
Tupas also submitted his sworn affidavit addressing the allegations of Gracioso.

In his affidavit, Tupas said that he used to be a City Information Officer of Davao City from July 1, 2016 to Nov. 8, 2021 and also worked in the Office of the Vice President from June 30, 2022 until Oct. 15, 2025.

“I felt so much surprise and shock when I saw in the media and social media the statements of Gracioso, and especially when I received a copy of his sworn statement where there were allegations that he, allegedly, delivered suitcases of money, gifts and vehicles to former Mayor of Davao City and now Vice President of the Philippines, Sara Z. Duterte, many times and he even implicated my name because he had stated that he had allegedly delivered or given me the (money) he delivered for the Vice President,” Tupas said in his sworn affidavit.
Tupas maintained that the allegations of Gracioso were “all lies.”

“In my entire life, I have never been to the house of former Speaker Lord Allan Velasco in Valle Verde or anywhere else and I do not know ‘Kuya Tony’ who was also mentioned in the sworn statement of Gracioso,” Tupas said.
According to Tupas, he does not know Gracioso, and accused the former policeman of trying to destroy the name of Duterte.

“As I said, I am now a private person and I no longer have any position in the government. Because of this, I want a quiet life and I hope that I will not be implicated again in fabricated stories, especially stories whose overt purpose is only slander and political wrangling,” Tupas added.
Duterte’s camp also debunked Gracioso’s claims of cash deliveries.

“He mentioned a specific date—Holy Week of 2019—but Jeff Tupas was in Korea at that time. Then there was another date—in 2021—but Jeff Tupas was in Japan during that period. Gracioso is just unlucky; whenever he fabricates a story, it happens to coincide with a time when Jeff Tupas—the person he claims he handed the suitcase to—wasn’t even around,” Duterte’s spokesperson Paolo Panelo said over Bilyonaryo News Channel.
DOJ: Gracioso statements ‘under evaluation’
The Department of Justice (DOJ) has vowed to study the allegations made by Gracioso on the deliveries of cash to the Duterte family on orders of Velasco.
In a media briefing yesterday, Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida said that Gracioso’s statement, which the agency received last week, remains “under evaluation.”

Should the need arise, the DOJ would study whether or not Gracioso could be admitted to the Witness Protection Program, as well as case buildup against personalities he accused in his affidavit, he added.

“We need to e able to validate and verify material points in his statement… we are seeing from open sources that some people were validating, some people were disputing, so the DOJ will scrutinize this,” Vida said.
Vida maintained they would look into the “totality of circumstances” surrounding Gracioso’s statements, considering the questions on his police record, including his dismissal already raised earlier.
– Bella Cariaso, Ghio Ong

articles.title: Trump dismisses low poll ratings as ‘fake numbers’ in Time interview
articles.summary: President also doesn’t rule out declaring state of emergency before midterms and deflects responsibility for Iran war

blocks.text: Donald Trump deflected responsibility for misleading Americans about the length of the Iran war, dismissed low poll ratings as “fake numbers” and refused to rule out the possibility of declaring a state of emergency before the midterms, in a wide-ranging interview with Time magazine.

When confronted with questions about the length of the Iran war, the US president blamed the media for reporting his remarks in which he said the conflict was projected to last “four to five weeks”, in March.
“ … I think the press fed it to them,” Trump told Time when asked whether Americans misunderstood him.
At the end of March, Trump had told Americans he planned to wind down the Iran war over the next “two to three weeks”. In May, Trump insisted that a peace deal with Iran was nearly finalized.
The US president said that he could have ended the Iran conflict whenever but chose to extend it “because I wanted to go further”.

For more than seven months, Americans have been grappling with higher everyday costs as a result of Trump’s war with Iran – from gas prices surpassing $4 per gallon to stubborn inflation hovering at 3.4%.

Economic concerns, fueled by Trump’s conflict, have angered voters, most of whom say they are unhappy with the president’s handling of the economy and his job overall. Just 26% of adults said they approve of the economy under the Republican president, according to an Associated Press/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.
Overall, just 31% of people said they approve of Trump’s handling of his job as president.
But when asked about his low approval rating during his interview with Time, Trump dismissed concerns.
“They’re fake numbers,” Trump said. “I would beat anybody running today by 20 points. Your numbers, that you have, are fake. The pollsters are corrupt. They’re almost as corrupt as the writers.”
The US president added: “See, I’m doing very well. I think I am. Look, we have the strongest economy.”
Despite Trump’s assertion, Americans do not feel the same way.
Approximately 74% of Americans told AP/NORC that the economy was leaning poorly. Another 65% of survey respondents said they blame Trump’s policies directly for higher costs.

Voters’ frustrations with Trump could affect Republican candidates in the upcoming midterm elections, particularly those closely aligned with the US president. Polls show many Democratic candidates making progress with voters, even in historically conservative states such as Texas.
Trump brushed aside the likelihood of Democrats winning, telling Time magazine that, so long as he campaigns with candidates, Republicans could perform well.
after newsletter promotion

Some Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns that Trump will again make allegations of election fraud if Democratic candidates outperform Republicans in the November elections. Trump refused to concede the 2020 presidential election after losing to Joe Biden.

In the months leading up to the midterms, Trump has claimed US elections are insecure and signed executive orders seeking to assert more control over voting methods – such as restricting mail-in ballot voting and requiring ID.

He has previously refused to rule out declaring a national emergency around elections to implement his desired regulations. Other administration leaders, such as the FBI director, Kash Patel, have not ruled out the possibility of deploying federal law enforcement officers to polling locations, which is against the law.
When asked whether he would declare a state of emergency before the midterms, Trump told Time magazine: “I don’t rule anything out or in. We’ll see.”

Trump further specified that while he’s never invoked the Insurrection Act, a 19th-century law that allows the president to deploy military troops domestically under specific circumstances, he “could use it”.
“A lot of people think I should use it sometimes,” Trump said.

Among other topics the president discussed with Time magazine, he responded affirmatively when asked whether he regretted appointing supreme court justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett.
“What can I do? I put them in. They voted against me too often. I was very – I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they voted against me often,” Trump said.

The supreme court often votes in favor of the Trump administration but it has ruled against the president – such as in the case challenging his sweeping tariffs and his efforts to roll back birthright citizenship.

articles.title: Renee Good's family sues U.S. government, ICE officer and others over Minneapolis killing
articles.summary: Lawsuits filed by Renee Good's family allege wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations in the 37-year-old's fatal shooting by a U.S. immigration officer during an immigration crackdown in…

image.caption: Renee Good was fatally shot by a U.S. ICE agent on Jan. 7, 2026, as protests against immigration raids flared across Minneapolis. (Tim Evans/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Lawsuits filed by Renee Good's family allege wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations in the 37-year-old's fatal shooting by a U.S. immigration officer during an immigration crackdown in January.
Lawsuits allege wrongful death, conspiracy in fatal January shooting by U.S. immigration officer

Renee Good's family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials on Thursday, alleging wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations in the 37-year-old woman's killing by an immigration officer during a federal crackdown in Minneapolis.
The two lawsuits were filed by Good's partner, Becca Good, and Renee's brother, Brent Ganger.
The U.S. Justice Department didn't immediately respond to an email seeking comment on the lawsuits.

Renee Good, a mother of three, was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbours during an immigration operation.

items: Renee Good's brothers mourn loss of 'beautiful American'
Investigating Renee Good's death is now up to the county — and no one else

blocks.text: Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver's seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.

Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, "Get out of the car."
Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: "Drive, baby, drive!"
One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him.
The officer, now very close to the open window on the driver's side, opens fire two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defence and that Good had engaged in "an act of domestic terrorism."
Moment of silence held at scene of Renee Good’s death days after Minneapolis ICE shooting
Lawsuits allege wrongful death and conspiracy

The lawsuit against the United States seeks damages for Good's wrongful death and "the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life, and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family," according to a news release filed by lawyers for Becca Good and Ganger.
The lawsuit also alleges "intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent infliction of emotional distress" on Becca Good.

Becca and Renee Good were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Mo. It asks for a bench trial.
The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights and seeks a jury trial.

items: ICE nodding to far-right extremists in recruitment posts, experts say
ICE detains 5-year-old boy coming home from Minnesota preschool

blocks.text: It says the shots fired by Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who killed Good, "were the predictable and intended product of the operation," which the lawsuit describes as a "carefully planned, co-ordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors to make two ethnic communities — Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin — the object of aggression and abduction, and to silence by intimidation, arrest and violence the neighbours and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented and warned of that campaign."

The lawsuit also alleges "collaboration of federal agencies and individuals with private entities for an operation with discriminatory design, racially targeted pursuit and seizure of individuals without regard to their legal status, and each defendant's participation in the conspiracy."

It names Ross as a defendant, as well as White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem, former U.S. Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino, former campaign manager Corey Lewandowski and others.

The killing of Good and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during U.S. President Donald Trump's second term.
'Should never happen to any family'

In social media accounts, Renee Good described herself as a poet, writer, wife and mom. On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child, alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.

In an interview shortly after her death, Renee Good's mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: "She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn't even understand … until we lost her."
"As we have tried to navigate our own massive loss, I am also devastated by how many other lives have been destroyed in this darkest of times," Becca Good said in the news release on Thursday.

"So many other families are dealing with the loss of their loved ones; to everyone who has had to witness it — the pain of this moment extends far beyond our family. What happened to us should never happen to any family."

articles.title: Crude oil exports from strait of Hormuz largely return to pre-war levels
articles.summary:
Alternative ways being used to move fuel out of Gulf region, but flows of refined products such as diesel still constrained

Exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned…

blocks.text: Exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war, as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.

Pipeline exports and ship-to-ship transfers are among the methods being used, according to analysts tracking the situation, while the US military continues to escort some vessels. However, flows of refined products such as diesel remain constrained, pushing prices higher.

At least 16.5m barrels per day (bpd) left the region in September, according to figures from the global trade intelligence firm Kpler, equalling the pre-war average, excluding Iran. The figure is 10.5m bpd higher than the monthly average for March, during the first weeks of the Iran war.

Since the conflict began on 28 February with US and Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran has sought to exert its authority on the strait of Hormuz and has at times even declared the strategic waterway closed.
However, Iran’s control appears to have declined in recent weeks, as oil exporters have found workarounds to address the disruption.

About 40% of the region’s crude is now transported without transiting the strait, compared with just 17% before the war, through Saudi and Emirati pipelines, according to Kpler analysis. Saudi Arabia was able to restart operations on its east-west pipeline in late September, after it was damaged during drone attacks, allowing exports from resume from the Red Sea port of Yanbu.

In a sign of the other adaptations, the majority of crude transported through the strait of Hormuz is carried on a shuttle fleet mostly comprising very large crude carriers, sailing with their satellite transponders turned off. The cargo is moved on to different tankers in open water, usually off the coast of Oman or Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates.

blocks.caption: Tankers and merchant vessels anchor off Fujairah. Ship-to-ship transfers are among the methods being used to transport oil. Photograph: Barry Iverson/Alamy

blocks.text: More than 70% of the crude that passed through the strait in August changed tankers, whereas before the war almost no Gulf crude changed ships in the Gulf of Oman.
However, the recovery in exports from the region remains unbalanced, and supplies of refined products remain constrained.
This poses a problem for businesses and households that depend on refined products such as diesel to run their cars, vans and lorries.
The average diesel price in the UK hit an all-time high of 199.18p a litre on Monday, with many motorists already reporting prices above £2 on some forecourts.
“Diesel carries the sharpest risk,” said Kpler analysts, who found that less than 20% of pre-war levels of refined products shipped through Hormuz were being transported.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The average diesel price in the UK hit an all-time high of 199.18p a litre on Monday. Photograph: Jacob King/PA

blocks.text: They recorded a seven-day average of 677,000 bpd of refined products as of Monday, compared with 3.6m before the conflict.
Even as oil exports from the region have increased, the level of threat to ships operating around the strait of Hormuz has not disappeared.

“New routes emerge, cargos are rerouted, risk is priced in and absorbed. The danger is assuming that resilience equals security. It doesn’t,” said Richard Meade, the editor in chief of shipping publication Lloyd’s List. “Oil flows have recovered because the market participants have accepted greater operational complexity and higher costs. The underlying threat remains.”
The danger to vessels and their crew was highlighted on Tuesday, when three Liberian-flagged tankers were hit by projectiles while transiting the strait.

The price of crude remains at elevated levels and moved higher again on Thursday, as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports with uncertainty over a long-term solution to the conflict and reopening of the strait.
The price of Brent crude briefly was back above $100 a barrel on Thursday, up 3% to $101.

The rise came after reports that China had suspended exports of oil products to regions beyond Hong Kong and Macau, a move that would add further pressure to oil markets. Oil analysts said China’s decision could suggest it was concerned about the availability of domestic products.

articles.title: Tennessee halts executions after death row inmate Christa Pike survives hers
articles.summary: Christa Pike was transported to hospital after the failed attempts. Her condition remains unknown.

blocks.text: Executions in Tennessee have been halted for the rest of the year, Governor Bill Lee has said, after two attempts to execute death row inmate Christa Pike by lethal injection failed.

In a statement to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, Lee said lawful executions were among the state's "most serious responsibilities", adding that he has ordered a third-party review "to determine exactly what occurred".
Tennessee prison officials on Wednesday attempted to administer two lethal doses of pentobarbital to Pike but she survived and was taken to hospital. Her medical condition is unclear.
Pike, 50 was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.
She was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer.
Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in Tennessee for over 200 years.
Speaking to reporters at a ribbon-cutting ceremony on Thursday morning, Lee said: "I'm highly disappointed, along with Tennesseans, about what happened last night."
Governor Lee has not made clear who will conduct the independent review of the state's execution procedures.
His order to pause all executions will overlap with the planned 3 December execution of convicted murderer Gary Sutton.
In court filings, Pike's lawyers said she needed "life-saving measures" after her botched execution.
The Tennessee Department of Correction, which handled the execution, issued a statement defending its handling of the case.
"The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office," the statement said.
"The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening."
This is the second time in 2026 Tennessee officials attempted and failed to execute a prisoner.
In May, the execution of Tony Carruthers was called off after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug. Carruthers was given a one-year reprieve.

articles.title: Canada Malting plant could collapse at any moment, engineering report says
articles.summary: According to an engineering firm's report, the Canada Malting plant in Montreal's Sud-Ouest borough could collapse at any moment. The report states “controlled demolition is the only possible, safe…

image.caption: The Canada Malting company site along the Lachine Canal in St-Henri was built in 1902. It was sold in 1980 and has been abandoned for 30 years. (Elias Abboud/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal·New

According to an engineering firm's report, the Canada Malting plant in Montreal's Sud-Ouest borough could collapse at any moment. The report states “controlled demolition is the only possible, safe and rational solution to eliminate the critical danger that this building represents.”
Report recommends demolition, threat of falling debris forces street closure near plant
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 01, 2026 11:42 AM EDT | Last Updated: 19 minutes ago
The Canada malting plant, which looms over Montreal’s Sud-Ouest borough and is notably home to the mysterious “pink house,” could collapse at any moment, according to a new engineering report.

The report, commissioned by the City of Montreal, says the structure — a mass of brick and concrete silos towering over the Lachine Canal to its south and Saint-Ambroise Street to its north — represents an “imminent danger” to public safety.

“Controlled demolition is the only possible, safe and rational solution to eliminate the critical danger that this building represents,” wrote the report’s authors, from the engineering firm STP ING inc.

Engineer André Houle, who wrote the report, is especially concerned about a facade wall, which he says has detached from the roof and is “hanging by a thread.” He’s worried about this brick facade falling onto Saint-Ambroise Street, where people walk and cars are currently parked.
“The only way to protect the public with this project right now is to close the street, there’s no other way,” Houle said in an interview with CBC.
The danger of collapse could worsen in the winter or spring, his report says. Freeze-thaw cycles could contribute to the collapse, as could vibrations from an earthquake.
Private developer ready to build
The engineering report is the latest development weighing on the future of the structure, which has lain vacant since 1985.
In a media release, La Malterie inc., a subsidiary of Renwick, the company that owns and plans to develop the site, said a demolition request had been submitted to the city.
Part of Saint-Ambroise Street will be closed in the meantime.
"The former Canada Malting site occupies a unique place in the history of Saint-Henri and in Montreal's industrial legacy,” Noam Schnitzer, the president of Renwick, said in a statement.
“We remain fully committed to ensuring that the identity of this iconic site can be live on through the future La Malterie project.”

La Malterie Inc. said its plan for the site includes 685 housing units, 20 per cent of which would be social housing. The plan also includes community spaces, businesses and community services. The company says it will also preserve the “pink house.”
The developer, the city and the community group À nous la Malting have clashed over the future of the site for years.
The group wants to turn the building into a collectively owned complex with 200 affordable rental units, a rooftop garden, a bike repair shop, a public daycare, a community kitchen and a museum.
Members of the group camped outside the plant in 2023 to protest Renwick’s development plan. They had pushed for the site to be used exclusively for social housing.
The malting plant and elevators were built in 1905 by the Canada Malting Co. Large cement silos were added in the 1940s to store barley.

The company exported the malt along the Lachine Canal, and when the canal closed to commercial navigation in 1970, the transportation cost rose to the point that the company abandoned the site in the 1980s.
Since then, it has fallen into disrepair. Windows are boarded up, brick walls are crumbling, and the facade is covered in graffiti.

And, though Renwick has set up barriers to prevent people from entering the building, it is popular with “urban explorers” and is home to the “pink house” — a small shack, painted pink and well maintained, which sits atop the crumbling plant.
Engineer says street should have closed earlier
Houle says he’s amazed people are still going into the building, given how dangerous it is. He described arches, made of bricks and steel, that have become especially hazardous.
“When that structure is rusted, it doesn’t hold the brick anymore and the brick falls on the ground,” he explained. “Left and right, the bricks are falling on the ground.”
The STP ING inc. report released Thursday warns that anyone entering the building risks death. In images, the report shows falling bricks and floors that are worn through.
Houle believes the area should’ve been closed one week ago. CBC News has reached out to the City of Montreal for comment.

“Anywhere else it would be, ‘we’ll close off the street and we’ll do the paperwork after. Because the safety is an issue,’” he said. “Here, we’re saying to the owner, ‘no… you need to go through the approval process.’”
“When it’s an urgent matter, there’s a safety issue, why do you have to work for the paperwork to be able to act?”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Matthew Lapierre is a journalist at CBC Montreal. He previously worked for the Montreal Gazette and the Globe and Mail. He can be reached at matthew.lapierre@cbc.ca and at mlapierre.07 on Signal.

articles.title: Netanyahu says flight attacker 'underwent Islamist radical indoctrination'
articles.summary: Israel's prime minister says the pilot who tried to take over the Flydubai plane clearly intended to "down the plane".

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".
The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.
Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu also said it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".
Passenger Almog Itali said it felt like a "rollercoaster" as Flight FZ1073 fell 17,000ft in less than two minutes

The co-pilot is currently being questioned in Saudi Arabia, where the plane made an emergency landing. However UAE officials say they have jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.

Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal that's not a question".

"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think ... that'll give us a pretty good clue but again I don't make final conclusions yet but that's the indications we have now."
The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".
The attacker was arrested in Saudi Arabia and is expected to be transferred to the UAE, Netanyahu said.
Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero".
India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well".

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"

blocks.text: Image source, Embassy of India in Israel
The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"
Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.
The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.
Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.
Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.

blocks.caption: Map showing the route of Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The plane departed Dubai at 03:05 GMT and flew northwest across Saudi Arabia towards Israel. Near the Israel-Jordan border, the aircraft declared a general emergency at 05:31 and a hijacking alert at 05:38 before turning away…

blocks.text: At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.
Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.
Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.
Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers.
The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

articles.title: Democrats are gaining ground. Could Trump still try to curb who can vote?
articles.summary: Five weeks from now, Americans will cast their ballots in the midterm elections to decide who controls Congress, and right now, Democrats have reason to be encouraged. Washington correspondents Katie…

image.caption: An attendee wearing a blue hat and American flag scarf attends the first day of the Democratic National Convention at the United Center on Aug. 19, 2024, in Chicago. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Radio·Podcast

Five weeks from now, Americans will cast their ballots in the midterm elections to decide who controls Congress, and right now, Democrats have reason to be encouraged. Washington correspondents Katie Simpson, Willy Lowry and Paul Hunter take a look at where the midterm races are heating up, what's at stake for Republicans and Democrats, and just how worried Trump might be.
5 weeks from now, Americans will cast midterm ballots
Five weeks from now, Americans will cast their ballots in the midterm elections to decide who controls Congress, and right now, Democrats have reason to be encouraged.

Some of the key Senate races are unfolding in Michigan, North Carolina, Alaska and Iowa. Democrats could gain roughly 20 seats in the House and about four or five in the Senate, according to Charlie Cook, founder of the non-partisan Cook Political Report.

But the road to election day is anything but settled. As Republicans fight to hold on to Congress, questions are growing about how far the Trump administration could go to shape the election — including the rules around who gets to vote.

Last Friday, the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for states to use an expanded federal database to check voter rolls, granting President Donald Trump a temporary win in his campaign against non-citizen voting.
So what could the decision mean for the midterms, and what other steps could Trump take before voters head to the polls?

Washington correspondents Katie Simpson, Willy Lowry and Paul Hunter take a look at where the midterm races are heating up, what's at stake for Republicans and Democrats, and just how worried Trump might be.
We've included some highlights below, edited for length and clarity. Listen to the full podcast discussion here.
Paul Hunter: With all these numbers and polls pointing toward Democrats, I think a lot of people worry, ‘Is Trump gonna push extra hard in other ways to try to salvage a win out of all this?’
A lot of talk centres around whether Trump will claim voter fraud and whether he will take steps to change the way people vote to the benefit of Republicans.
What do you know about that?
Willy Lowry: He set the scene for that over the summer when he had that primetime address, which raised all of these concerns that the administration had over election integrity.

Much of them were eventually refuted over the course of the preceding days, but he is already trying to plant the seeds of doubt for sure. The Supreme Court, recently, is going to allow something that the administration called for, which is to allow states to use a new system of data that combines citizenship information with social security number and other sensitive data points to try and essentially hunt out illegal voters.
But the Supreme Court [is] also ruling against the administration, which was trying to use the postal service to screen ballots after they were submitted by the state election officials.
The Supreme Court's saying [that] introducing new rules around mail-in ballots at this point would have wreaked havoc, sowed chaos, [therefore] denying the administration's request.
Katie Simpson: Donald Trump has a clearcut history of trying to undermine integrity in elections, so that if there is a result he doesn't like, that perhaps no one believes the result.
Look what happened after January 6, and he's set himself up to continue that pattern heading into the midterm elections as the polls do not look to be in his favor.

With all of these complicated things that the federal government is trying to do to insert itself into these elections — which as a reminder to Canadians, they are actually run by individual states, not the federal government.

[So] why would the federal government — or the Trump administration — want these states to have this information? It's to possibly knock people off voter registration so that they can't vote or they have to sign up or that maybe they missed their deadline.
In one county, in Texas, there is an example where people were erroneously knocked off a voter list.

Is this the Trump administration trying to make it harder for people to vote, who might not want to vote for the Trump administration? Is it easier for the Republicans to win should fewer people show up or they're disenfranchised to vote? Is the Trump administration gonna do something by sending ICE agents or military officials to polling stations, which they cannot [legally] do.
Paul Hunter: Is Trump losing, or are Democrats winning? Or can both be true? What are Democrats doing to win this thing?
Katie Simpson: This is a moment for the Democrats to try and determine which route they're going to go in 2028.

They've got a slate of really progressive candidates, they've got a slate of more moderate candidates, and depending on the outcome and who can get elected, I think it's really going to be the litmus test for which route they go for candidates to be the presidential candidate in 2028.

Also, this is not specific to the Democrats, but it really applies to the Democrats, given the track record of the party over the past decade or so: don't underestimate the ability of a party with a lead to screw up a lead. The polls may suggest that the Democrats are gonna do very well … but there is so much time, and we don't know whether the Trump administration is gonna have any ability to disenfranchise voters.
Willy Lowry: At this point, the Democrats’ best strategy is a little bit [of] ‘Get out the way and let this all unfold — let the price of gas keep rising.’
I don't view it as a vote against Trump, because I think he still holds a really captivating sway over the Republican Party, and yet, it is a vote against his agenda and his policy decisions.

In particular, the U.S.-Iran war — not only was it a betrayal of a campaign pledge to avoid wars, but more importantly, it is having that direct impact on Americans' wallets, and I think that's what this is about.

articles.title: Finland probes suspected break-ins at politicians' homes
articles.summary: The Finnish prime minister has not ruled out the possibility of foreign involvement in the suspected break-ins at the homes of members of parliament.

image.caption: Officials are speaking of a "significant" number of break-ins and attempted intrusions at the homes of several MPs [FILE: March 2023]Image: Heikki Saukkomaa/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Finnish police are investigating a series of suspected break-ins at the homes of members of parliament, officials announced on Thursday.
Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo was asked by a reporter if a foreign power could be behind the suspected intrusions, and he replied that it was "very possible... quite possible in these times."
"If someone tries to destabilize Finland, our sense of security, or our support for example for Ukraine, it has the opposite effect. It strengthens our unity," he added.
Meanwhile, Finnish President Alexander Stubb stated, "An attack against a member of parliament is an attack against democracy."
What do we know about break-ins?

After the media reported on the alleged intrusions, speaker of parliament Jussi Halla-aho confirmed that parliament had been made aware of a "significant" number of break-ins and attempted intrusions at the homes of several politicians.
"I cannot comment precisely on the number of suspected cases known to us, but in any event, it is significant," Halla-aho said at a press conference.
He added, however, that the known cases had occurred over a longer period of time, with the first believed to have taken place about a year ago.
Halla-aho also emphasized that, at this point, no information is available about the motive or the perpetrator.
Paula Risikko, the deputy speaker who leads the parliamentary security group, said she was informed of the suspicions last week.
She added that the Helsinki police had been tasked with the initial stage of the investigation.
A night in Finland's largest underground defense bunker
MPs advised to keep an eye out
Earlier this week, newspaper Ilta-Sanomat reported that MPs had been warned of potential break-ins and that the newspaper was aware of at least two home intrusions.
All members of parliament were told to keep an eye out, report any suspicious activity, and file police reports if necessary.
Helsinki police confirmed that a preliminary inquiry had been opened. "The inquiry is at an early stage, and the police have nothing further to comment on at this time," it said.

Since the Kremlin began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Finland has been on high alert. The Nordic country, which shares a 1,340-kilometer (830-mile) border with Russia, abandoned its decades-long policy of military non-alignment and joined NATO in April 2023.
Finland previously accused Moscow of "hybrid warfare" and orchestrating a surge of migrants at their shared border in 2023. The Kremlin denied the allegations.
Edited by Zac Crellin

articles.title: This is how fast Swiss glaciers, the 'water tower of Europe,' are melting away
articles.summary: Glaciers in Switzerland lost 5.5 per cent of their ice volume this year, the second-biggest percentage drop on record. It's part of a trend that could have big impacts in a country reliant on…

image.caption: Tourists gather at the glacier-feed Oeschinensee lake near Kandersteg, Switzerland, on Aug. 4. The country's glacier-monitoring service says Switzerland lost the second-highest percentage of glacier ice on record this year. (Hernan Munoz/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Science·New

Glaciers in Switzerland lost 5.5 per cent of their ice volume this year, the second-biggest percentage drop on record. It's part of a trend that could have big impacts in a country reliant on hydropower and which acts as the 'water tower of Europe,' feeding its major rivers.
Water lost so far this year is 4 times Switzerland's annual consumption

Glaciers in Switzerland — the home to the most in the Alps — lost 5.5 per cent of their ice volume this year, the second-biggest percentage drop on record due to heat waves and low winter snowfall, experts report.
"Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions," the GLAMOS Swiss glacier monitoring service and Swiss Academy of Sciences said in a statement Thursday.
The trend has worsened in recent years. Over the past five years alone, the volume of ice in Switzerland has declined by nearly a fifth, the experts say.
The report testifies to the latest concerns that global warming is wreaking havoc on Europe, the world's fastest-warming continent.

"The warming that we are experiencing now can be attributed 100 per cent to anthropogenic climate change. It's as simple as that," said Matthias Huss, who heads GLAMOS. "Without human emissions or fossil fuels we wouldn't have any warming at the moment."
Why low snowfall was a big problem

The record retreat of glacier ice in Switzerland came in 2022, when summer heat, low winter snowfall and an unusual smattering of reddish dust blown in from the Sahara darkened the glaciers and caused them to absorb more heat.
Huss said the snow cover in winter was important for two reasons.

"On the one hand, it protects the bare ice from melting. The longer you have snow, the longer you avoid the loss of old ice," said Huss in an interview at the Federal Polytechnic Institute ETHZ, where he is a glaciology professor.

"On the other hand, the snow is important also for generating new food for the glacier. The more snow you have, the higher the potential to keep some of the snow at high elevation and to form new ice."
Satellite images show glacier collapse that triggered flooding at Nepal-China border

The great thaw in Europe's legendary Alps is not alone: Experts say global warming helped to destabilize a Himalayan slope that collapsed in August and unleashed catastrophic and deadly flooding across Nepal. Satellites have shown vast shrinkage of glaciers in places like Greenland and Antarctica over the last half-century or so.

In Switzerland, in absolute terms, volume lost has been less than that in 2003, but the percentage decline this year is greater. That's because the total volume today is roughly a third of that 23 years ago. Back then, the relative loss was 3.5 per cent of total ice volume in Swiss glaciers.
What happens if Canada's thickest glaciers disappear?

Such accelerated ice melt has had an impact in Switzerland — the loss of 2.2 trillion litres from July to September amounts to four times the annual consumption of water in the country of about 9.1 million people. Switzerland gets more than half of its electricity from hydropower.
But the impact of accelerated glacier melt ripples far beyond: Switzerland is the water tower of Europe, and feeds some of the continent's most important rivers: the Danube, Po, Rhine and Rhone.

The experts say the "extreme melting" faced by Switzerland's glaciers this year included a decline in the average thickness of individual glaciers between two and half and four metres — and a reduction of up to 10 metres on the tongue of some glaciers.
Which glaciers saw the biggest melt
The expert teams have fanned out to assess runoff and crevices caused by the running water through the glaciers, in part by dumping red dye into the streams to track the water flows.
The Allalin, Clarident, Rhone and Aletsch glaciers — Aletsch being the largest in the Alps — were among the glaciers to experience their biggest melt on record this year.
"We just need to stabilize the climate by reducing CO2 emissions and this will help the glaciers," said Huss, of GLAMOS, though he added that it is "almost too late" to save those in the Swiss Alps.

"For the ice in the polar regions like the ice sheets, there it's not yet too late," he said. "There, we can make a difference and we need to make a difference in order to limit sea level rise, for example, a factor that is a fundamental threat to billions of people living along the coast."

articles.title: Canadian Olympian Claire Thompson retires from PWHL to pursue medical career
articles.summary: Defender Claire Thompson, one of Canada's top women's hockey players, is retiring from the sport to become a doctor. The 28-year-old played with the PWHL's Vancouver Goldeneyes last season.

image.caption: Former Goldeneyes defender Claire Thompson set an Olympic record for points by a defender with 13 at the 2022 Beijing Games and finished with 17 points in 14 career Olympic games. (Ethan Cairns/Canadian Press/File)

blocks.text: PWHL·Updated
Defender Claire Thompson, one of Canada's top women's hockey players, is retiring from the sport to become a doctor. The 28-year-old played with the PWHL's Vancouver Goldeneyes last season.
28-year-old defender played 2 seasons in league with Frost, Goldeneyes
One of Canada's top women's hockey players is retiring from the sport to become a doctor.
Defender Claire Thompson announced her retirement Thursday on Instagram and in an exclusive interview with The Athletic.
The 28-year-old Toronto native won Olympic gold with Canada at the 2022 Beijing Games and silver earlier this year in Milan after putting her medical career on hold for two years.
Thompson set an Olympic record for points by a defender with 13 in Beijing and finished with 17 points in 14 career Olympic games.
She also won the Walter Cup with the PWHL’s Minnesota Frost in 2025 before spending last season with the expansion Vancouver Goldeneyes.

“A career in medicine has always been an overarching goal of mine and I feel that now is the best time in my life to step away from hockey,” Thompson told The Athletic. “I have achieved far more than I could have ever hoped for and I feel like I’m ready to step away and continue on the long road ahead of becoming an orthopedic surgeon.”
Thompson has returned to medical school at New York University.

In 2024, she had started school and hoped to also practice with the PWHL New York franchise (now known as the Sirens) when the league officially began play. But it wasn't a viable option, so Thompson chose hockey.
Helped Frost to second straight title
She declared for the 2024 PWHL draft and was selected third overall by the reigning champion Frost.
Thompson adjusted quickly following her time away from the game and was one of the PWHL's top defenders, helping Minnesota to a second consecutive title.

“That was such a fun run,” she recalled to The Athletic. “I feel so lucky to have been drafted by Minnesota … I really feel like it was just a fortunate happenstance that they took a chance on me after the year off."

items: Goldeneyes sign No. 1 PWHL draft pick Caroline Harvey to 3-year deal
PWHL hires hockey attorney Alison Izzi to be Goldeneyes GM

blocks.text: Thompson joined the Goldeneyes for the 2025-26 campaign, becoming the first player in franchise history and an alternate captain.
She scored and added an assist in Vancouver’s first game, played in front of a deafening crowd of 14,958 at Pacific Coliseum.

"Getting to play in front of Canadians and living back in Canada was something that was also really special,” said Thompson. “To be able to play my last season in Canada, in front of Canadian fans, was amazing.
She also represented Canada at the 2025 world championships and captured a silver medal.
