articles.title: Weakened US fuel-efficiency rules and promises of cheaper cars could see drivers pay higher running costs while also increasing carbon emissions.
articles.summary: Weakened US fuel-efficiency rules and promises of cheaper cars could yet see drivers pay higher running costs while increasing planet-heating emissions.

image.caption: Gas prices are on the rise as Trump moves to make cars less fuel efficientImage: Mario Tama/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: As part of its "Freedom Means More Affordable Cars" initiative, the US Department of Transportation this week rolled back fuel efficiency rules under the guise of lowering vehicle prices.

The Trump administration's transport agency says US taxpayers will save $138 billion (€122 billion) over the next five years — new vehicles will be $1,300 cheaper on average — since automakers will no longer have to invest in more fuel-efficient fleets.
But this does not account for soaring gas prices as Middle East conflicts choke global supply.

"Any savings on the front end get eaten up and spat out by excess costs of fuel … Fuel economy standards have saved drivers hundreds of billions of dollars," said Democratic Senator Sheldon Whitehouse in a social media post.

Under the revised Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) rules, vehicle fleets only require an average fuel efficiency of about 35 miles per gallon (14.7km per liter) by 2031, down around one-third from 50 miles per gallon.

Implemented by the Biden administration in 2024, the updated efficiency rules aimed to incentivize the production of low emission electric vehicles and hybrids. The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) estimates the standards would have saved 70 billion gallons (265 billion litres) of fuel over 25 years.

blocks.caption: Drivers in the US will be pumping more gas under weakened fuel efficiency rules Image: Brandon Bell/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: Meanwhile, nonprofit advocacy group, the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) says an earlier version of CAFE regulations has saved US consumers have saved about $321 billion at the gas pump since 2010.
Rollbacks set to increase planet-heating emissions

The world's biggest petrol consumer, the US burns through 20 million barrels of oil per day, which is 20% of global consumption, notes Dan Becker, director of the Safe Climate Transport Campaign at the US-based nonprofit environmental group Center for Biological Diversity.
"Transportation is the biggest consumer of that oil, making strong auto standards the most effective way to cut pollution and oil use," Becker said in a statement.

The rules that have been diluted this week would have prevented more than 710 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions by 2050 — the equivalent of running 165 million gas-powered passenger vehicles for a year.

"With transportation representing nearly 28% of US greenhouse emissions, rolling back fuel economy standards is a dangerous setback for near-term climate goals," said Ben Scott, head of Energy Demand at UK-based climate think tank, Carbon Tracker.
"It risks keeping inefficient combustion engines on the road much longer than climate science demands," he told DW.

But following the Trump administration’s elimination of greenhouse gas emissions standards for light- and heavy-duty vehicles last year, Dave Cooke, senior vehicles analyst for the UCS Clean Transportation Program, said the rollbacks merely compound "a much more significant step backwards."
He said the trend sends "a specific signal to automakers," adding that "the United States is seeking to maximize oil usage to increase oil company profits."
This will be to the detriment of climate targets, with high-polluting oil contributing one-third of global fossil fuel emissions that continue to rise — along with temperatures.
The world just had the hottest August on record as severe heatwaves in Europe caused over 16,000 excess deaths in Germany alone.
US turns its back on EVs
Can US transport still transition to clean energy?
Sales of low emission EVs are down in the US in 2026, especially after president Trump scrapped the $7,500 tax credit for new electric vehicles.
American automakers also continue to push back against regulations that would incentivize a switch to EVs, arguing there is a lack of consumer demand.

"It's highly unlikely that the United States will suddenly become awash in electric options when neither the auto industry nor regulators seem interested in providing such choices for consumers," said Cooke.
But Ben Scott believes that while softening US fuel economy standards "will create temporary headwinds", it won't stall an inevitable transition to electric vehicles.

"With EVs delivering vastly lower running costs, electrification becomes a clear-cut economic choice," he said of cars running on "cheaper, domestically secure energy that will drive the transition forward, regardless of short-term politics."
As less efficient cars and trucks consume more oil that's more expensive and in shorter supply, "the fragility of oil-dependent transport" is set to be exposed, he said.
Trump vs. the US auto industry

articles.title: Poll suggests slight majority of UCP voters favour separation as party stares down ‘tough days’ ahead
articles.summary: A new poll suggests the group with the highest level of support for Alberta separation is supporters of the United Conservative Party, trumping other groups, including those defined by age,…

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks to party faithful at the United Conservative Party annual general meeting in Calgary on Nov. 4, 2023. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: As part of her latest round of polling, Janet Brown sought to understand the factors driving support for separatism in advance of Alberta's Oct. 19 referendum.
She found most support wasn’t found amongst people who live outside the major cities.
It wasn’t the majority opinion of people with a certain level of education.
Nor was it of those who work a certain type of job or make a certain amount of money.
The group where the highest levels of support for Option 2 was found? Supporters of the United Conservative Party.
“It is a hot potato for the UCP and Danielle Smith. It is that part of the voting public that is split on this issue,” she said.
On Oct. 19, voters will be asked whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada, or whether the Government of Alberta should hold a second, binding referendum to separate from Canada.

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage
Everything you need to know about the 10 questions in Alberta's Oct. 19 referendum

blocks.text: Among those polled who said they would vote for the United Conservative Party, 53 per cent said they’d vote for the separation option. Forty per cent said they’d vote to stay in Canada.
That trumped all demographic groups studied by Brown and her team.
Compared to the 53 per cent of UCP supporters in favour of the separation option, 25 per cent of respondents in small centres said they’d vote for Option 2 on Oct. 19.
Twenty-eight per cent of those with a high school education or less supported the separation option, while 30 per cent of those with college or some university said the same.
At 98 per cent, nearly all respondents who said they would vote for the Alberta NDP if an election were held today said they wanted to stay in Canada.
“I’m a little bit surprised to see them that high in the UCP, very admittedly,” Travis Toews told CBC News of the numbers.
Toews was Alberta's minister of finance from 2019 to 2023. He’s one of the signatories to the federalist initiative known as Lead Not Leave.
He sees “lingering scar tissue” in the party tied to former federal policy.
“I think many of us were disillusioned during those years,” Toews said.
But he argued conditions have improved under Prime Minister Mark Carney.
“It’s a different day. We now have … the majority of Canadians supporting energy development and pipelines,” he said.
“Over time, we can agree with a majority of Canadians on key economic issues that not only will affect Alberta's prosperity down the road, but quite frankly, the whole nation's.”
Still, Toews sees the political clouds swirling. The divide between the two camps in the party poses challenges in advance of the next election, in his view.

“I think if we continue to have a preoccupation — if right of centre provincial political parties continue to have a fixation with separation and independence — I believe it will make it very difficult for those parties to form government provincially,” he said.
“These are tough days for Premier Smith politically, for sure.”
On Tuesday, Red Deer-South UCP MLA Jason Stephan confirmed to CBC News he has voted in favour of proceeding with a legally binding referendum on whether the province should leave Canada.
“I've always supported having a referendum on independence because I want Ottawa to be compelled to fix the things that are broken," he said.
He added, “I've never said that I want Alberta to separate."
Last month, the Alberta NDP flipped a conservative stronghold with a win in Calgary-Shaw.
Later that week, a UCP riding association in southern Alberta formally urged a party vote to review the premier’s leadership.
“Here’s the reality: this kind of an issue is very divisive. And it’s divisive within communities, within businesses, within families and certainly within constituency associations,” Toews said.
“We need to get through this, past this referendum. I believe that we as Albertans need to rally around the principle of leading, not leaving.”
Warring flanks of United Conservatives

It was Highwood, a riding south of Calgary, that was first out of the gate calling for a party vote of the premier’s leadership. Forcing such a vote would require the support of a total of 22 associations.

items: UCP riding group demands leadership review as separatist leader criticizes Danielle Smith's unity stance

blocks.text: Tanya Clemens, co-leader of the separatist group Let Alberta Decide, is part of the Highwood association.

She told CBC News that while she tends to doubt conservatives are accurately represented in polling, she believes there is a “large, silent group” of members that are in support of separation but who fear backlash should they vocalize that opinion.
She said she supported the leadership review given Smith’s stance that Alberta should remain in Canada.
“I just want to ensure that, as much as I love and respect her, that if we win Option 2 on Oct. 19, that she is then accountable to the people to deliver on that mandate,” Clemens said.
“And that would be to then call the independence referendum for the spring of 2027.”
There may be more constituency associations that similarly endorse a leadership review, UCP president Rob Smith wrote in a comment on Facebook.
“But it’ll never make 22. I bet my house on it!” he wrote.
“There’s also a movement of constituency associations writing letters of support for Premier Smith. That number will exceed 22 within a week or two! And it’ll get much, much higher!”

It’s within the two flanks of her party — those who feel she has not sufficiently supported their efforts to separate and those frustrated that the referendum is taking place at all — where Smith faces her biggest challenge, in pollster Janet Brown’s view.
“Both sides … are agitated right now,” she said.
Premier says discussions will follow referendum

Lisa Young, a professor of political science at the University of Calgary, noted that the poll also suggested that Smith’s personal popularity dipped as her party found itself tied in support with the Opposition NDP.

items: Danielle Smith’s popularity dips as her party now tied with NDP in support: poll

blocks.text: While the premier has consistently said she supports a sovereign Alberta within a united Canada, voters may perceive her as being on the other side of the issue, Young said.
Over the longer term, she sees a real challenge for the UCP, given that separatist movements typically want to have a political party that can further their objectives.
“I think what we’re going to see over the coming weeks and months is a fight over whether the UCP becomes an overtly separatist party,” Young said.
“If it does, it cedes potential support, because there are conservative-minded voters who wouldn’t vote for an explicitly separatist party.”
At an unrelated press conference on Wednesday, Smith was asked about the poll’s findings and how she planned to manage fissures in her party.

“It'll all be decided on Oct. 19. So at that point, we're going to ensure that we have a very robust discussion with Albertans about accepting the results and what it means, as well as how we're going to continue to pursue greater autonomy for Alberta," Smith said.
“So that is going to be a discussion to have with Albertans, and also a discussion to have internally in our party.”
In a statement responding to the poll results, a UCP spokesperson said “Albertans have real frustrations with Ottawa,” and the party is working to prove that Canada can work for Albertans.

“That means getting a pipeline built to the West Coast, scrapping the production cap, the net-zero electricity rules, and holding Ottawa accountable for implementing the energy agreement,” Dave Prisco said in an email.
“There's still more work to do and we will continue defending our economy and constitutional rights while restoring hope for all Albertans.”

When it came to all respondents to the poll, 23 per cent said they’d vote to start the legal process to hold a binding referendum, while 72 per cent said they’d vote to remain in Canada. Four per cent said they were unsure.

The CBC News random survey of 1,200 Albertans was conducted using a hybrid method between Sept. 8 and Sept. 21, 2026, by Edmonton-based Trend Research under the direction of Janet Brown Opinion Research. The sample is representative of regional, age and gender factors. The margin of error is +/- 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.

The survey used a hybrid methodology that involved contacting survey respondents by telephone and giving them the option of completing the survey at that time, at another more convenient time, or receiving an email link and completing the survey online. Trend Research contacted people using a random list of numbers, consisting of 30 per cent landlines and 70 per cent cellphone numbers.

Telephone numbers were dialled up to five times at five different times of day before another telephone number was added to the sample. The response rate among valid numbers (i.e., residential and personal) was 11.3 per cent.

articles.title: Can Trillanes hold a presser after withdrawing as impeachment trial witness?
articles.summary: Is former senator Sonny Trillanes covered by the sub judice rule, or the ban on parties from discussing the merits of the impeachment case outside the trial proceedings?

blocks.text: Published October 1, 2026 6:53pm

Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV on Thursday asked the House prosecutors to withdraw his name from being a witness in the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, saying he would hold a press conference instead.
But is Trillanes covered by the sub judice rule, or the ban on parties from discussing the merits of the impeachment case outside the trial proceedings?
One law expert, San Beda University law professor Adonis Gabriel, said that whatever Trillanes will say in his upcoming press conference cannot be considered as evidence.

"Technically hindi siya evidence na iko-consider ng impeachment court sa pagde-desisyon. Kaya lang, again, sui generis ang impeachment trial. Mailalahad na ni former senator Trillanes kung ano yung mga impormasyon na gusto niya ipresenta sa impeachment trial," he said in an interview with Pia Arcangel.

(Technically, it would not be considered evidence that the impeachment court must consider in its decisions. But again, this impeachment trial is sui generis [in a class by itself]. [At the press conference,] former senator Trillanes will be able to divulge what information he wanted to present at the impeachment trial.)

Gabriel said the former senator is not covered by the sub judice rule as he is not an involved party or a counsel in the trial. Hence, the trial will not be compromised if he decides to make statements during a press conference.

"Hindi covered si former Senator Trillanes nung sub judice rule...kung hindi siya partido, hindi rin siya counsel. Pwede niyang gamitin yung karapatan niya bilang mamayan na right to freedom of speech, freedom of expression,” he told GMA News.

(Former senator Trillanes is not covered by the sub judice rule... he is not a party [to the trial], nor is he counsel. He can exercise his right as a citizen to freedom of speech and freedom of expression.)
The law professor said that Trillanes would have more freedom to share what he can as compared to a trial witness.
“Which is mas malawak 'yan kaysa sa karapatan ng mga testigo sa impeachment trial. Dahil walang mag-o-object, walang magde-determine ng kung ano ang extent ng pwede niya isiwalat,” he added.

([His ability to speak at the press conference will be] broader than the rights of witnesses in an impeachment trial. Because no one will object, and no one will determine the extent of what he can disclose.)
At their press conference on Thursday, members of the House prosecution and private prosecutors panel said the public should watch Trillanes' press conference.
"Let us watch [former] senator Trillanes' presscon tomorrow," House lead prosecutor Representative Gerville Luistro of Batangas said.
Earlier this week, the prosecutors sought Trillanes to stand as their next witness in relation to funds and bank accounts as the impeachment court tackles Duterte's alleged unexplained wealth.
However, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis "Chiz" Escudero rejected the request to subpoena Trillanes.
Likewise, Ateneo Policy Center senior research fellow Michael Henry Yusingco said the sub judice rule only covers those involved in the trial proceedings.
"The sub judice rule only covers the senators, the respondent, and the counsels on both sides. It doesn't cover the public," he told GMA News Online in a message.

The Senate impeachment court decided to move the next trial session to Monday, October 5 after it granted the defense panel’s request to prepare for prosecution’s direct examination of Anti-Money Laundering Council executive director Ronel Buenaventura. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Raffy Tulfo calls out prosecution over 'palpak, nagpapa-cute' presentation of witnesses
articles.summary: Senator judge Raffy Tulfo on Thursday called out the prosecution for supposedly screwing up in certain moments of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published October 1, 2026 6:52pm
Senator judge Raffy Tulfo on Thursday called out the prosecution for supposedly screwing up in certain moments of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Tulfo made the manifestation Thursday during Day 32 of the impeachment trial of the vice president.

"Kasi kung minsan, 'yung prosecution, sorry ah, pero palpak palpak kayo. There are times na naglalagay kayo ng mga witnesses dito na hindi naman kailangan talaga. Nagsasayang tayo ng oras," Tulfo said, without dropping names.
(The prosecution, sorry, but sometimes you screw up. You fielded witnesses that are not needed. It is a waste of time.)

"Wala eh, parang useless eh. So [kung] kukuha kayo ng witness, make sure na talagang witness na iyon, mayroong masasabing bagay na makatulong sa ginagawang investigation sa impeachment. Meron pa kayong kinuha, pinagtatawanan tuloy, nagpapa-cute lang habang may kinakausap na witness na police," Tulfo added.

(It appears useless. When you field a witness, you should ensure that it would shed light on the impeachment allegations. You even had a lawyer who was just trying to look cute while talking to a witness who is a police.)

It was House prosecutor Bel Zamora of San Juan who questioned the Police Major Jerickson Sangalang, Records Division chief of the Philippine National Police Firearms and Explosives Office on the guns owned by the Vice President and her husband, Manases Carpio.
Zamora asked the police official if it was appropriate for the vice president to have 22 guns, but it was objected upon by the defense for being speculative. The court ruled in favor of the defense.
"So, ingat kayo sa pagkukuha ng mga witness at ingat kayo sa pagsasalang ng mga abogado ninyo diyan," Tulfo said.
(You should be cautious in fielding witness and lawyers doing the questioning.)
'Walang nagpapa-cute'
In response, the prosecution panel said members of the prosecution team have always been serious in proving the allegations in the impeachment case against the vice president.

"With all due respect to our senator-judges, I believe that all the members of the prosecution panel are working very hard to be able to present very well the evidence for the prosecution. I hope we will not be judged on the basis of minor, nonsense, totally irrelevant observations," House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro of Batangas said in a press conference.

"Wala pong nagpapa-cute rito. Kung meron mang nagpapa-cute, mas mabuti pong pangalanan po siguro. As far as we are concerned, we are focused on the case, we are proud of our prosecutors," House prosecutor Terry Ridon of Bicol Saro party-list added.

Private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan, for her part, said senator-judges should be reminded that the Senate should be a safe space for all, including women, since it was instrumental for the passage of the Safe Spaces Act or Bawal Bastos law.
"It could be a misstatement [on the part of Senator Tulfo], but I still believe that the Senate is a safe space, [including] for woman and senior citizens like me," Kapunan said. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Jonvic Remulla did not say Marcoses are ‘sure to be jailed’ after 2028
articles.summary: There is no credible record showing the interior secretary saying that the Marcoses are afraid of a member of the Duterte family assuming the presidency in 2028

blocks.text: Claim: Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Secretary Jonvic Remulla said President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his son, House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, would be jailed if a member of the Duterte family becomes president in 2028.

Why we fact-checked this: A viral quote card features Remulla’s photo and attributes a supposed September 19, 2026 statement to the interior secretary: “Pag hindi na presidente si BBM Marcos [sigurado] makukulong sila kasama si Cong Sandro Marcos kaya takot sila pag pamilya Duterte umupo presidente sa 2028. Ako marami ako alam sa kalokohan ni presidente.”

(If [Bongbong Marcos] is no longer president, they will surely be imprisoned, including Cong. Sandro Marcos. That’s why they are afraid of having a member of the Duterte family assume the presidency in 2028. I know a lot about the President’s wrongdoings.)

The graphic was posted by two Facebook users with over 17,000 followers each. One of the posts received 3,400 reactions, 464 comments, and 995 shares, while the other had 4,100 reactions, 457 comments, and 921 shares.
On TikTok, the account “byahevlog tv” also shared the same graphic, which garnered 21,900 views, 190 reactions, 62 comments, and 31 shares as of writing.
The facts: There is no credible evidence that Remulla made the statement attributed to him.

A search of credible news reports and publicly available government records found no interview, press briefing, speech, official statement, or social media post in which Remulla said the President and his son, Sandro, would be jailed if a Duterte family member becomes president in 2028.

The graphic is dated September 19, 2026, but the posts carrying it were published on September 21 and 22. Neither post identifies where or when Remulla allegedly made the statement, and neither provides a video, interview, transcript, speech, or news report showing him making the remark.

On September 19, Remulla spoke about the Banga National High School shooting in South Cotabato, which occurred the previous day. He discussed the shooter’s alleged involvement in the “deep dark web,” the firearm used in the attack, and possible government measures following the incident. None of his documented remarks that day contains the statement circulating in the viral graphic.
Remulla on the 2028 elections: Remulla has made public remarks about the 2028 presidential race, but none of his statements match the quote in the viral posts.

In March 2026, Remulla was asked who could challenge the 2028 presidency bid of Vice President Sara Duterte. He named Senators Bam Aquino, Risa Hontiveros and Raffy Tulfo, as well as former vice president and Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo, while declining to answer whether he would personally run. Remulla later said he was undecided about his plans, but was inclined to run for a local seat in Cavite. – Vic Albert Bagaan/Rappler.com
Vic Albert Bagaan is a petroleum engineering student at Palawan State University in Puerto Princesa City, Palawan. The editor-in-chief of Pioneer Publication, he is an Aries Rufo Fellow for 2026.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Tennessee governor halts executions after second botched lethal injection attempt this year – US politics live
articles.summary: Bill Lee pauses state’s remaining executions for the rest of the year after inmate Christa Pike survives two lethal injections

blocks.text: Tennessee governor halts executions after second botched lethal injection attempt this year
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Tennessee governor Bill Lee has halted the state’s remaining executions for the rest of the year after officials were unable to put Christa Gail Pike to death yesterday.

Pike, 50, was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and taken by ambulance from the prison, her attorneys said. She was being treated at a hospital, but they said they hadn’t been told about her condition.
She had been scheduled for execution at 10am on Wednesday for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
Governor Lee said that he was halting the one remaining execution for the rest of 2026 and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.”

“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” Lee said in a statement.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that they “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office.”

Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said in court filings late Wednesday. The state’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.

It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to carry out an execution. In May, state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried and failed for over an hour to place an IV to administer pentobarbital.

blocks.text: Trump officials abandon effort to investigate election threats, experts warn

blocks.caption: George Chidi

blocks.text: George Chidi

The Trump administration has abandoned key security bodies meant to investigate direct threats to US elections by foreign actors and domestic terrorists, according to former officials and a recent report.

While administration officials have been actively focused on unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud by noncitizens, other credible election threats appear to have been overlooked, the officials say.

Between 2021 and 2024, the justice department’s election threats taskforce prosecuted 21 cases, like that of Solomon Peña, a failed candidate for the New Mexico house of representatives who organized shootings at the houses of election officials, or Quintez Brown, who shot up a campaign meeting of Louisville’s mayor.

Democrats and Republicans faced prosecution for harassing, intimidating and threatening elections workers, noted Nikki Fisher, former chief election security officer for the Oregon secretary of state, now the executive director of the Oregon District Attorneys Association.
Since then, the taskforce seems to have gone quiet.

“While officials are being trained to handle threats, the federal deterrent meant to punish the people making them appears to have gone quiet,” Fisher said. “To date, no new cases have been prosecuted, and the DoJ’s election threats taskforce appears to be defunct in practice.”

articles.title: UAE launches flydubai hijacking and terrorism investigation
articles.summary: The UAE's chief prosecutor said it's looking at the possibility of "terrorist activity or intent" in the alleged attempted hijacking of a flydubai commercial flight to Tel Aviv. It says it has…

image.caption: A replacement plane brought the passengers safely to Ben Gurion airport late on Wednesday Image: Gil Cohen-Magen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The United Arab Emirates' chief prosecutor's office said on Thursday that it had ordered an investigation into the apparent attempt to hijack and possibly crash a flydubai flight to Israel a day earlier.

The state news agency WAM said that "the investigation team has launched its work into the incident already" and that the probe would seek to determine "the degree to which [the incident] was linked to any terrorist activity or intent."
The case will also seek to establish whether it was a pre-meditated and planned incident involving other actors or the work of a lone perpetrator.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz had called the emergency on the flight to Tel Aviv "an attempted jihadist terror attack" that was thwarted.
Passengers described rushing the cockpit to assist the pilot after he was stabbed by his copilot, who then put the plane into a steep dive in an apparent attempt to crash the airliner.
Aside from minor curts and bruises among those who intervened in the cockpit, the passengers — the vast majority of whom were Israeli — were all unhurt.

blocks.caption: Israeli passengers returned home late on Wednesday after the near-missImage: Ohad Zwigenberg/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why does the UAE have jurisdiction in the case?
Judicial authorities in the UAE have jurisdiction over the incident.

This is because the aircraft is registered in the UAE and flies under its flag, the statement said, adding that UAE law applied to crimes committed on board "even if they occur outside the country's territory."

The plane was over northern Saudi Arabia for the majority of the early-morning security incident, with tracking data suggesting it briefly crossed into Jordan before turning around to make an emergency landing at the nearby Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.
FlyDubai passengers recount terror after hijacking attempt
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had also indicated the likelihood of the UAE leading any investigation in a TV interview with Fox News.

"The attacking pilot is ... now being investigated in Saudi Arabia. I think he'll be taken to the Emirates, where he comes from, or at least where he left, where he flew off from, and we'll be following and possibly also participating in this investigation," Netanyahu said.

The Omani copilot's identity has not been made public as yet and his motive is not clear. US President Donald Trump said that based on a discussion with Netanyahu, he understood that the suspect was "perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack-job."
Asked about the possibility of Iranian involvement amid the conflict in the Gulf, Netanyahu said "it's too early to say."

blocks.caption: Israeli leaders spoke to the passengers who intervened in the cockpit, like Yaniv Hayoun speaking here to Prime Minister Benjamin NetanyahuImage: GPO/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Israel's Herzog nominates 4 passengers for presidential medal
Israeli President Isaac Herzog plans to nominate four passengers who helped overpower the attacker for the Presidential Medal for Civil Courage.
Herzog and Netanyahu spoke with the passengers when they arrived at Ben Gurion Airport on a replacement flight late on Wednesday.
Herzog named the passengers as Yaniv Hayoun, Shota Musayev, Zvika Manes and Asaf Rajuan.
"You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disater," Herzog said. "Today, the whole world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society."
The medal is Israel's highest civilian award for heroism. Herzog confers the medal but typically nominees are formally chosen by a committee.
Musayev, a dentist who administered first aid to the severely wounded Indian pilot, told Herzog everyone on board had acted courageously.
"We supported one another on the plane and also when we arrived in Saudi Arabia, and we took care of each other as we should," he said.

blocks.caption: Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu hailed Captain Smit Machchhar's 'extraordinary bravery'Image: Israel's Foreign Ministry/AFP

blocks.text: The Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, has also received staunch praise from Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and from India's Narendra Modi. Passengers described how the pilot fought off his attacker despite his wounds and was able to open the cockpit door to let them in to aid him. He was in a stable condition in a Saudi hospital, India's Embassy in Riyadh said on Wednesday.

"In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others," Modi said online. "His valor helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy."

articles.title: Why is Rosary Month celebrated in October?
articles.summary: As the Catholic Church dedicates the entire month of October to praying the Rosary, the faithful are urged to seek the intercession of the Our Lady of the Rosary and contemplate the life of Jesus…

blocks.text: As the Catholic Church dedicates the entire month of October to praying the Rosary, the faithful are urged to seek the intercession of the Our Lady of the Rosary and contemplate the life of Jesus Christ through the mysteries.
During his Apostolic Journey to France, Pope Leo XIV urged the faithful to pray the Rosary for peace, particularly in the world’s conflict areas.
“Let us accompany this prayer with concrete acts of penance and mercy, committing ourselves always to fostering dialogue and reconciliation,” the Pontiff said.
But why is the Rosary Month celebrated in October, and how did the veneration of the Marian image begin in the Philippines?
An October victory

Pope Pius V established the feast of the Our Lady of Victory, the name of the Our Lady of the Rosary then, on October 7, 1571, after Christian forces won a battle against the Ottoman Empire in the Gulf of Patras in western Greece.
The victory weakened the Ottoman Empire’s westward expansion and helped prevent its potential conquest of Christian Europe.

In an interview, historian Br. Dennis Amarante, O.P., of the Order of Preachers, said Pope Pius V asked the faithful to seek the Blessed Virgin Mary’s intercession for the victory of Christian forces by praying the Rosary.

“Pope Pius V, who was a Dominican, asked the people, and he himself, prayed the Rosary to ask the intercession of the Blessed Mother in order for the Christian forces to prevail,” Amarante told GMA News Online.
“And they did prevail. So they won the naval battle. And as a result, in thanksgiving, Pope Pius V instituted October 7 to be the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary,” he added.
In 1573, Pope Gregory XIII changed the name of the feast from Our Lady of Victory to the Feast of the Holy Rosary to honor the power of the Rosary used during that battle.
Since the Feast of Our Lady of the Rosary falls in October, the entire month eventually became known as the Rosary Month.
Filipinos’ faith in the Rosary
After the victory in the Battle of Lepanto, the praying of the Rosary was soon introduced in the Philippines after the Order of the Preachers (Dominicans) arrived in the country in 1587.

"One of those missionaries who came to the Philippines was the Dominicans, and being the primary propagators of the Holy Rosary, they brought the veneration to the Marian image in the country,” Amarante said.
He shared that when the Dominicans arrived in the Philippines, they brought a statue of Our Lady of the Rosary and housed it in the Sto. Domingo Church in Intramuros, Manila.

“When Santo Domingo Church was still standing in Intramuros, it was there in the façade. Unfortunately, one of the casualties of the Second World War,” said Amarante, who published articles and conference papers on Philippine Church history, Philippine Dominican history, and historical methodology.

An image of Sto. Domingo Church in Intramuros, Manila, before it was destroyed during the bombing in World War II. The image is displayed at the Museo de Santo Domingo in Quezon City. Mariel Celine Serquiña/GMA News
For Catholics, praying the Rosary is a way to seek healing, solace, and comfort while reflecting on the life of Jesus Christ.
The Rosary is divided into four sets of mysteries: the Joyful, Sorrowful, Luminous, and Glorious Mysteries. Each set consists of five events from the life of Jesus Christ.
As they meditate on each mystery, Catholics pray the Hail Mary 10 times, followed by one Glory Be.

For Amarante, despite the Marian image’s Western iconography, it eventually took on a local context in the Philippines, with devotions to Our Lady of La Naval de Manila in Quezon City, Our Lady of Manaoag in Pangasinan, and Our Lady of the Rosary of Orani in Bataan, among others.
"Eventually, over time, it would have a significant effect on the lives of Filipinos. Filipinos would eventually call her their own,” Amarante explained.
One reason, the Dominican brother said, is that the Marian image “transcended the bounds of the context” to which Filipinos can relate.

“They see not just a Western icon or statue, but they see it as a representation of the Blessed Mother who is there with them despite challenges and tribulations, guiding them towards her Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. Each of them would carry their own prayers of supplication,” Amarante said.
Lessons from Our Lady of the Rosary
Like the Blessed Virgin Mary, Amarante challenged the faithful to be courageous in doing good and be devoted to God and his teachings.
"Pinakita ng Mahal na Ina na kahit na maraming pagsubok, kahit na ang daming pagihirap, dumipende siya sa kanyang pananampalatay sa Diyos," Amarante said.
(The Blessed Mother showed that despite the many trials and hardships, she relied on her faith in God.)
"Ginawa niya ang tama, sumunod siya, at namuhay siya bilang isang mabuting hapo, isang mabuting ina, isang mabuting pananampalatay," he added.
(She did what was right, obeyed, and lived as a good person, a good mother, and a woman of faith.)
In a time where there is violence, division, dishonesty, and disregard for what is right, Amarante said it's easy to show "religious fervor."
"Sa panahon ngayon, ang dali-daling mag debosyon, ang dali-daling magpakita ng religious fervor, we always depend on the externalities of things," the Dominican brother said.
(In these times, it is easy to practice devotion and show religious fervor, but we often rely too much on the external aspects of our faith.)

"So sana, sa patuloy nating pamumuhay bilang mga Kristiyano na may debosyon sa Mahal na Birheng Maria, sana yung mga lessons na yun maglulot sa atin ang internal transformation, conversion," he added.
(So, as we continue to live as Christians devoted to the Blessed Virgin Mary, may the lessons we learn from these devotions lead to an internal transformation and conversion.)
Follow facebook.com/gmanewsonline for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.—RF, GMA News

articles.title: Alex Eala runs into Chinese wall anew, settles for Asian Games bronze

blocks.text: RETURN. Tennis player Alex Eala in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.

Top seed Alex Eala sees her gold-medal bid in the 2026 Asian Games end at the hands of China's Wang Xiyu as she replicates her bronze finish in the 2023 edition

items: Filipina tennis player Alex Eala won a bronze medal at the 2026 Asian Games after losing in the semifinals to China's Wang Xiyu.
Eala, ranked No. 18 in the world, had high expectations but faced a tough match, ultimately losing 3-6, 6-3, 6-2.
Despite the disappointment, Eala expressed pride in representing her country and is looking forward to competing in the upcoming Wuhan Open.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Another one of the Philippines’ top gold-medal bets in the 2026 Asian Games fell as tennis star Alex Eala settled for a bronze on Thursday, October 1.

For the second straight edition, the Filipina ran into a Chinese wall, suffering a 3-6, 6-3, 6-2 loss to Wang Xiyu in the semifinals of the women’s singles at the Higashiyama Park Tennis Center in Nagoya, Japan.
“A lot of good points, a lot of tough moments for me. I think in the end, she played better. Have to sit and think about it,” Eala told Filipino reporters.
Eala replicated her bronze finish in 2023 in Hangzhou, China, where she also lost in the semifinals to Chinese star and eventual champion Zheng Qinwen.
This time, though, expectations and scenarios were different as Eala came in as the highest-ranked player in the field at world No. 18, even earning a first-round bye as the top seed.
And Eala lived up to her billing at the start, racing to a 5-0 lead before holding off a Wang comeback to clinch the opening set.
But Wang, ranked 85th in the world, proved to be no pushover as she won the second set to force a decider and went on to complete the upset victory in 2 hours and 34 minutes.
Down 1-4 in the third set, Eala showed signs of life by breaking Wang in the sixth game, but that only delayed her exit as the Chinese won the next two games to seal the win.
A forehand error by Eala marked the end of her gold bid.

It was a disappointing result for Eala, considering she entered the tournament as the title favorite, with the likes of Zheng, world No. 1 Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan, and world No. 17 Naomi Osaka of Japan skipping the Asian Games to compete in the China Open.

The loss denied Eala a shot at becoming the first Filipino tennis champion in the Asian Games since Johnny Jose ruled the men’s singles in 1962. It also denied Eala a direct entry in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
But as dismayed as she is, Eala relished the opportunity of representing the country again in a multi-sport showdown.

“It meant a lot to me to be here and to compete. At the end of the day, I gave my all. I prepped the best I could prep. I fought the best I could fight. Happy that I was able to have this experience,” she said.
Up next for Eala is the Wuhan Open that kicks off in China on October 12. – Rappler.com

articles.title: [READOUT] What Philippine borrowing tells businesses ahead of 2027
articles.summary: Here are three credit insights to keep in mind, covering consumer borrowing trends, business lending, and the national debt

blocks.text: It turns out whether you’re running a household or the country, debt is becoming a bigger part of the picture. For businesses though, what matters more than the mere fact that borrowing is rising is what that debt is being used for and whether enough value is generated in return.
Here are three points worth watching as you plan for 2027.

First, credit is becoming an important cash flow tool for Filipino consumers amid a challenging economic environment, and this could have implications for what payment options retailers should prioritize offering.

Rappler sat down one-on-one with Peter Faulhaber, president and CEO of TransUnion Philippines, whose latest Credit Perception Index reached a record 75 as Filipinos became more knowledgeable, trusting, and favorable toward credit overall.

But this growing comfort with borrowing is happening with a still-cautious consumer. TransUnion’s report found respondents less confident about their own finances over the next three months and one year. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) Q3 survey also showed consumers had weaker plans for day-to-day household spending even as their expectations for future income and employment improved.

A deeper look into the lending data helps explain how those two things can coexist. The BSP found that credit card receivables jumped 24.9% year on year to P1.3 trillion in July and salary-based general purpose loans rose 15.7%, while motor-vehicle loans grew just 4.5%. TransUnion, meanwhile, reported that buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) products had the strongest growth in adoption, with what Faulhaber called a “large take-up rate” and “strong favorability.”

The emerging picture: cash-strapped consumers may be using shorter-term loans to manage when expenses are paid, rather than simply to fund large purchases. Around 59% of credit users told TransUnion they borrow for emergency expenses, ahead of personal expenses and utility bills, a pattern Faulhaber described as a sign of greater maturity.

For retailers, that may mean rethinking which payment options get the most emphasis. BNPL, installments, and cards can help customers manage tight cash flow and avoid delaying a purchase. Some 43% of Filipinos surveyed said they plan to borrow or use credit to make purchases, up 5 percentage points from last year. BNPL was the credit product most commonly viewed as “helpful” at 54%, ahead of credit cards at 49%. Cost could limit uptake, however, with 54% citing high interest rates as a reason to avoid credit.
Second, in today’s difficult macroeconomic environment, business credit has become selective, but not weak.

Production loans remain almost five times larger than consumer credit at P13.2 trillion and account for roughly three-fourths of local bank lending, according to BSP data. But the fastest growth is concentrated only in particular parts of the economy:

items: Fastest growth came from infrastructure-linked industries. Water and waste loans rose 26.2%, transport and storage 25.1%, electricity and gas 24.4%, and accommodation and food services 16.3%.
The biggest loan books grew more slowly. Real estate rose 5.5% to P2.89 trillion, wholesale and retail 8.8% to P1.64 trillion, and manufacturing 7.2% to P1.28 trillion.
Construction was the clear weak spot. Loans fell 13.3% year on year to P447.5 billion.

blocks.text: Third, keep an eye on the national debt and how it could tighten fiscal space for everyone.

National government debt stood at P19.39 trillion in July, while financial expenses in the proposed 2027 budget reached P1.114 trillion. Neither the World Bank nor the economists Rappler spoke with sees an immediate debt crisis, given that much of Philippine debt is long-term, domestic, and peso-denominated.

The concern for business is the squeeze on fiscal space. Interest costs have risen from around 10% of government spending before the pandemic to about 16.7% today, leaving the Marcos administration less room to fund infrastructure and other projects that might have otherwise improved private sector productivity.

Rappler resident economist JC Punongbayan puts it neatly. “Borrowing for productive investments is defensible, but borrowing for overpriced, substandard, or ghost projects only worsens the debt problem.”
We hope this readout helps inform your next strategy or boardroom decision. And as always, feel free to tell us what to tackle next, dear business leader. – Rappler.com

Readout is a new content series from data consultancy The Nerve, bringing you insights that bridge the gap between quick news headlines and dense technical reports. Readout tracks and explains business shifts in different Philippine industries. Crafted from on-the-ground reporting and data-driven analyses, Readout provides a clear read on where market and consumption are headed, what’s shaping demand across different sectors, who the key players are, and why it all matters.

articles.title: Germans' biggest fear is the high cost of living, an annual study finds
articles.summary: What do Germans fear most in 2026? Wars? Global crises? Wrong. Their biggest concern is the cost of living, which keeps rising.

image.caption: Germans see the price of groceries, energy risingImage: Frank Hoermann/SvenSimon/picture alliance

blocks.text: People in Germany are more politically engaged than they have been in a long time. This was also evident in the high voter turnout in the September state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Germans are passionately debating immigration, the upcoming reforms to pensions, healthcare and long-term care, as well as democracy and the rule of law.

But by far their greatest fear is the cost of living in Germany, which is becoming increasingly expensive. At least, that is the finding of the 2026 study on "Germans' Fears," which the insurer R+V presented in Berlin.
From early May through late July of this year, researchers surveyed some 2,400 German-speaking citizens aged 14 and older.
The cost of living is again their top concern, as it has been in the survey for many years in a row. This study has been conducted annually since the early 1990s.
Last year, 52% of those polled cited the rising cost of daily life as their greatest concern; in 2026, that figure has risen to 59%.
At a press conference in Berlin, Isabelle Borucki, a political scientist from Marburg who served as a consultant on the study, explained why.
"The price of key items — energy, housing and food — has risen noticeably. This reduces the financial leeway for leisure, vacations and purchases. People can afford less and less."
Germans worry about higher taxes and contributions
The study also shows that people are well aware that Germany's social security systems are in a serious crisis. Both the state pension fund and long-term care insurance are chronically in the red.
Most people also seem to realize that taxes and contributions will rise. That is why the fear of higher taxes is stronger than in previous years.

"Behind the fear of higher taxes and benefit cuts lies the question of fairness, with people wondering who will bear the costs of modernization," Borucki said. "And they worry, 'Can I still rely on getting benefits I am entitled to?'"
Less fear of war, immigration and Donald Trump
But what about the issues that are also dominating the headlines in Germany? What about immigration and the increasing polarization of society? Or global upheavals?
A narrow majority of 52% of those surveyed fear that the number of refugees is overwhelming the German state. This fear ranks third among all concerns.
But when it comes to global upheavals, Germans are not so concerned.
Only 45% of respondents fear that US President Donald Trump's policies are making the world a more dangerous place, researcher Grischa Brower-Rabinowitsch said.
"That's significantly fewer than during his first term."

In 2018, during Trump's first term, 69% responded to the same question by saying that this made them very afraid. "After years of constant geopolitical alarm bells, people are starting to get used to it," Brower-Rabinowitsch said.
Berlin has space, so why is housing so expensive?
German politicians got poor grades

This trend also seems to hold true for other areas of concern: Germans are looking to the future with considerably less anxiety than expected. Only 34% now fear a war involving Germany, down from 41% last year.

Since 1992, the study has asked people if they are afraid of losing their job? Currently, only 20% of the surveyed members of the working population answered "yes." That is the lowest figure ever recorded.

However, the assessment of politicians — both those in the government and those in the opposition — is sobering: Respondents were asked to grade politicians with one being the best and six the worst (the grading system used at German schools). The result was an average score of 4.1, which is barely a passing mark.

Political scientist Borucki places the primary responsibility on the current government of conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) under Chancellor Friedrich Merz which came to power in May 2025.
After the end of the previous coalition government, many associated the new coalition with hopes for more leadership, less conflict and a rapid economic turnaround.
"That has not come to pass," says Borucki. "There is now a gap between the grand announcements and tangible results. People are disappointed and losing confidence."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Pakistan launches deadly airstrikes on Afghanistan
articles.summary: The Taliban government in Afghanistan said at least nine civilians were killed in Pakistani airstrikes on two provinces overnight. Pakistan said it had struck militant hideouts, killing 22 fighters.

image.caption: The Taliban said civilian homes were struckImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Pakistan launched airstrikes overnight on two provinces in neighboring Afghanistan, the two countries said Thursday.
The Taliban government in Kabul said at least nine civilians, all women and children, were killed, while 11 others were wounded.
Pakistani authorities, on the other hand, said the strikes had killed 22 militants. Neither casualty toll could be independently verified.
The airstrikes are the latest clash between the two neighbors since cross-border tensions spiked earlier this year.

blocks.caption: Pakistan accuses Afghanistan of harboring militants, which Kabul deniesImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: What do we know about the latest Pakistani airstrikes on Afghanistan?

The Afghan government spokesman said three civilian homes in the southern province of Helmand and in the eastern province of Kunar, which borders Pakistan, were hit, killing nine and injuring 11 others.
Residents of Helmand told the AFP news agency that three bombs had struck their village, and there is "no military or anything else" in the area.
"We condemn this act and consider this an act of aggression and a crime that violates all universally accepted principles," Zabihullah Mujahid said.

blocks.caption: Men salvage their belongings from the debris of a house in Kunar provinceImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Authorities in Islamabad, however, said that 22 militants had been killed, and that weapons and ammunition had been destroyed.
The airstrikes on militant hideouts were "well planned and calibrated" and were carried out "with precision and accuracy," Pakistan's Ministry of Information said.
"Maximum precautions were taken and it was ensured that no collateral damage occurs," the statement said.
What's behind the conflict between Pakistan and Afghanistan?
The strikes overnight are the third time in the past two weeks that Pakistan has hit targets in Afghanistan.
Simmering tensions since the Taliban seized power in 2021 erupted into open conflict last year​​​​​​.
The two countries held peace talks in April to shore up a March truce, but sporadic flare-ups have continued in the months since.
Islamabad accuses the Taliban government in Kabul of harboring militants who carry out attacks across the border in Pakistan, an allegation Afghanistan denies.
"The threat to Pakistan emanates from Afghanistan," Pakistan's information ministry said. "Our action precisely targeted the terrorist hubs."
Since the conflict escalated last year, Pakistan has closed its border crossings with Afghanistan, which is heavily reliant on foreign food and humanitarian aid.
Last week, the United Nations said more than 1,100 civilians had been killed or injured in Afghanistan as a result of the cross-border conflict this year.
Pakistan insists that it does not target civilians.
Are Pakistan and Afghanistan heading for war?

articles.title: ‘It’s utter surrealism’: Venezuela’s Chavistas lament government’s embrace of Trump
articles.summary:
Diehard Hugo Chávez supporters struggle to comprehend ideological U-turn being executed by Delcy Rodríguez’s interim administration

He was one of the most passionate propagandists for Hugo…
articles.byline: Camille Rodríguez Montilla in Caracas and Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: He was one of the most passionate propagandists for Hugo Chávez’s Bolivarian revolution: a feisty leftist TV personality who spent more than two decades singing the movement’s praises on his state-funded show, The Razorblade.
Mario Silva’s devotion was such that he often hosted his programme with Chávez’s portrait behind him and he had El Comandante’s curly signature tattooed on to his left wrist.

But nine months after Venezuela’s political landscape was scrambled by Donald Trump’s abduction of Chávez’s heir, Nicolás Maduro, Silva’s show has been cancelled, and its host is livid about the revolution’s direction under Maduro’s former deputy, Delcy Rodríguez.

“[I feel] a lot of disappointment – depressed … and sometimes I wake up and feel like the world is collapsing around me,” the 66-year-old said during a rare interview at his home studio in the mountains outside the capital, Caracas.

Silva has spent recent weeks railing against Rodríguez’s interim administration on YouTube, his home since his programme on state TV was axed, berating those he blames for Venezuela’s “shameful and utterly illegitimate surrender” to the US.

Since January, a parade of high-ranking US officials – including the head of the CIA, the chair of the joint chiefs of staff and the energy secretary, Chris Wright – have visited Caracas, while Trump recently trumpeted striking “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Rodríguez’s regime. Last week, Rodríguez and Trump met on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, posing for a smiley photograph that left diehard Chavistas such as Silva aghast.

“I thought it [the photo] was artificial intelligence or something like that. But it’s surrealism, utter surrealism … It’s impossible to understand,” Silva fumed on YouTube as a red flag emblazoned with the faces of Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels and Vladimir Lenin hung behind him.

blocks.caption: Mario Silva in his home studio in La Guaira state, Venezuela. Photograph: Andrea Hernández Briceño/The Guardian

blocks.text: “They have surrendered this country and surrendered it the most vile and despicable way,” Silva went on. “Honestly, they are dragging the country’s name through the mud. They are dragging Chávez’s name through the mud.”

In another broadcast, Silva seethed about the cosy post-Maduro relationship that has developed between one-time anti-imperialist flagbearers in Caracas and Trump officials: “Traitors and lackeys, you will have to answer for this!”

Silva is not the only Chavista loyalist struggling to comprehend the ideological U-turn being executed by Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president but has engineered a historic rapprochement with the US since his rendition on 3 January.

Elías Jaua, a vice-president and foreign minister under Chávez, is also up in arms, and claims the feeling is widely shared. “What I hear from comrades across the country is bewilderment, disagreement and indignation,” said Jaua, who believes Trump’s oil deal “amounts to an act of pillage against an entire nation”.

blocks.caption: Venezuela’s interior minister Diosdado Cabello addressing a crowd during a march in support of Delcy Rodríguez last week. Photograph: Diko Betancourt/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Juan Barreto, a former member of the ruling Socialist party (PSUV) and mayor of Caracas, said such an agreement would have been unimaginable when the Bolivarian revolution began after Chávez’s 1998 election. He said Chavistas, who had once vowed “Not a drop of oil to the empire if Venezuela is attacked!”, were now in effect saying: “All of the oil reserves [for the US], for as long as you want!”
“The current situation is one of tutelage,” Barreto said.

Rodríguez has defended the deal, claiming it will create more than $209bn (£158bn) in revenues that will help improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said in a recent TV broadcast.

Héctor Rodríguez, another prominent Chavista politician, has sought to deflect criticism of Venezuela’s interim government by recalling how Chávez was forced to make a tactical retreat after his failed coup attempt in 1992. “No one can tell me Chávez was a coward. He understood that the balance of power had shifted … and decided to take a step backwards,” Rodríguez said recently.

​Last week as Delcy Rodríguez met Trump in New York, thousands of people ​joined a pro-government rall​y in Caracas, where supporters parroted the slogan “Delcy avanza, tú tienes mi confianza!” (“Move forward, Delcy. I trust in you!”).

blocks.caption: Ex National Assembly deputy and television presenter Mario Silva in his home studio. Photograph: Andrea Hernández Briceño/The Guardian

blocks.text: “No matter how much they kick and scream, there’s nothing they can do to try to cover up the success of President Delcy Rodríguez’s visit to New York,” her interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, ​told the crowd. Unlike at previous marches, there was scant mention of Maduro and few calls for him to be released.
The depth and potential consequences of Chavista anger over Rodríguez’s embrace of Venezuela’s longtime foes in Washington remain unclear.

Orlando Pérez, a Latin America expert from the University of North Texas at Dallas, recognised there was indignation at what some considered a sellout of their anti-imperialist ideals. “There are Chavistas that are pissed off, there’s no question about it,” he said. “There are Chavistas who see this as a betrayal of Hugo Chávez and the betrayal of the movement.”

But Pérez believed that for many Chavistas who had remained in power after Trump’s invasion, the “pragmatic reality” was that working with Washington was “a necessary evil” if it meant keeping Venezuela’s opposition out of power.

“If that means negotiating with Trump, if that means dealing with the CIA etc, it’s fine,” he said. “Beyond whatever ideological position they might have … I suspect most of them are gritting their teeth and just going along with this process as long as they can stay in power and keep their jobs. I think for most it’s as simple as that: it’s about their material wellbeing.”

However, Pérez believed Rodríguez’s government would need to demonstrate to supporters “tangible benefits to the cooperation” with the US in order to avoid a backlash. “They’re going to have to show that these things have a material consequence to the lives of their social base … if you don’t deliver, then it is going to get very volatile,” he warned.

blocks.caption: A Venezuelan government supporter carries dolls depicting Hugo Chávez and the pro-government comic-book characters Super Bigote and Cilita at a march in Caracas backing Delcy Rodríguez’s participation in the UN general assembly in New York. Photograph: Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: So far there has been no sign of significant resistance from outraged supporters of Chavismo. But Silva claimed the government’s new direction and economic policies could eventually trigger a social uprising and protests.

“Worsening economic conditions will degrade [people’s] quality of life, and that pressure is bound to explode. It has to explode – it’s not just wishful thinking. This isn’t a prediction born of desire, it’s an inevitability,” said the broadcaster, who has claimed he is facing investigation for alleged acts of “aggravated defamation and slander against the interim government”.

Silva lit one cigarette after another as he recalled the early hours of 3 January 2026 when, as US troops swept into Venezuela’s capital, he realised the revolution he had spent more than 20 years defending was not going to defend itself.

The Chavista broadcaster said he moved from one strategic point to another across Caracas before finally calling the commander at his assigned post. “I said: ‘Hey, what happened? Where are the weapons?’” Silva recalled, his face settling into a sad grin as he remembered the answer. “Go to sleep, Mario,” he was told.
Silva pauses. “You have no idea how disappointed I was.”

articles.title: Why children in government care face a higher risk of sexual exploitation
articles.summary: Young people who are in government care can be prime targets for sexual exploitation, as demonstrated by recent cases in Nova Scotia courts. According to a senior Crown prosecutor, sexual predators…

image.caption: Kyesha Boudreau, 28, shared her story with CBC in the hope that it can help other people with current or prior experience as children in government care. (Brian MacKay/CBC)

blocks.text: Kyesha Boudreau spent part of her childhood shuffling through roughly 12 foster homes, leaving her with a painful sense that families had put her under a microscope and decided not to choose her.
“I feel like I got picked over,” she said in a recent interview at her home in Nova Scotia’s Annapolis Valley.
She firmly believes that pain set her up to be a target of sexual exploitation later as a teenager living in group homes.

items: Fear, sadness, and anger: Why children in N.S. government care frequently go missing

blocks.text: People who work with youth in government care have long understood these children are particularly vulnerable to human traffickers.

Court decisions as recent as December 2025 describe men buying and selling sex with girls who lived in Nova Scotia group homes, some as young as 14. According to a senior Crown prosecutor who worked on some of the cases, sexual predators found victims by lurking near the homes or scoping them out on social media. Many survivors now face “devastating long-lasting impacts.”
Boudreau, 28, said it's deeply upsetting a decade after her own experience that it continues to be a major issue in the child welfare system.

She believes children in group homes are the “easiest targets” for traffickers because when staff can't meet their emotional needs, youth turn to anyone offering “the slightest bit of love, affection, attention.”
How kids in Nova Scotia's group homes become trafficked

“All someone has to do that wants to pimp you out — I've seen it happen so many times and even in my own experience — they will come up to you, they'll offer you anything they know you want,” she said.
That’s why Boudreau thinks her longing to be chosen left her vulnerable to be picked for all the wrong reasons.
“A kid in care, they're going to see that as the best part because when have you ever been chosen? You're in a group home. You're obviously not chosen,” she said. “That's the sad thing.”
Gifts and social media
Human or sexual trafficking relies on coercion, meaning the trafficker uses threats or manipulation to force someone into providing sexual or other services.
Statistics Canada data from 2024 shows Nova Scotia had the highest rate of human trafficking of any province, at 4.5 police-reported incidents per 100,000 people.
Senior Crown attorney Katie Lovett, who has prosecuted more than a dozen human trafficking cases in Nova Scotia, said perpetrators look for targets lacking something in their everyday lives.
Those needs might be food, shelter, alcohol or drugs — or emotional support, such as a trusted adult to lean on.
“They will use that need to build trust with that person and eventually manipulate and exploit them,” Lovett said.

items: Halifax police lay human trafficking charges against 40-year-old man
More suspects, more charges in Halifax-area human trafficking case

blocks.text: She’s known traffickers to hang around gas stations or convenience stores near group homes. That gives them a chance to offer to buy the target something like a pack of cigarettes, opening the door for further contact or gifts. This can continue for months, Lovett said.
“Eventually they will stop and they will tell the person, I've bought you $500 worth of items in the past month, you need to pay me back,” she said.
Traffickers also use social media to approach teens and build trust.
By befriending a youth online, Lovett said, traffickers can check their friend list to identify others living in the same group home.
Location-sharing features on platforms like Snapchat create additional risks. If a youth has their location turned on, traffickers can track them on a map in real time.
Lovett said she’s also known of cases where teens have handed over access to their social media accounts.
“It might not be a long time period [of access], but for enough time for them to go on and try to make connections that they can use later on,” she said.
Subtle coercion
Ashley Tiller wants to dispel the myth that human trafficking involves a stranger snatching a victim off the street and forcing them into a vehicle.

“That sensationalized version is not how it commonly occurs,” said Tiller, who manages several gender-based violence support programs at the YWCA Halifax. “It's a lot quieter. It's a lot more subtle.”
The YWCA operates a peer support program and safe house for human trafficking survivors.
Trafficking can happen in the community where the victim lives, she said, and most cases involve women and girls who may take a long time to recognize the warning signs.
Tiller said that’s because the trafficker can often be a friend or romantic partner who excels at making the target feel loved and cared for.
“Maybe it's the two of them against the world together,” she said.
Tiller said the relationship slowly starts to shift, perhaps with the trafficker pushing different sexual experiences until the target agrees.
“Step by step, trying to push boundaries in a new way to make things that previously were outside of somebody's comfort zone on the table,” she said.
‘They’ll watch you for a few days’
Some traffickers set up situations where they can meet youth in person.
“They'll watch you for a few days. I literally had someone watch me and my friends on the bus,” Kyesha Boudreau remembers.
“All of a sudden we kept seeing him pop up every day in front of our group home. We didn't know who he was.”
She said staff warned the girls that the man was dangerous.
“We didn't believe them,” Boudreau said. “We're like, oh, you're just trying to scare us.”
But the warnings proved true.
“He would literally invite us to his apartment to hang out. He'd give us weed, he'd give us liquor, and then he'd take the bus home with us to make sure we got home.”
She knew that some of her friends were sexually exploited by the man.
“They would come home and tell me, 'yeah, maybe I shouldn't have stayed,'” she said.
“We would report it to the group home staff. They wouldn't do nothing about it because in their eyes, you did that to yourself. We told you about it and you still went and hung out with this person.”

Jill Barkhouse, executive director of the child and family well-being division at Nova Scotia's Department of Opportunities and Social Development, said staff act on every report of sexual exploitation and trafficking.
“We take those concerns seriously and we tend to those with actions,” she said, though she said out of respect for people’s privacy sometimes the actions aren’t shared or widely known.
Barkhouse said the department is working on public awareness campaigns and training for social workers, and working with groups in the community that fight against sexual exploitation.
She said as exploitation moves online, protecting children looks “very different than it did some time ago” and requires considerable skill and attention.
Healing and choice
Tiller emphasized that recovery programs at the YWCA allow survivors to lead their own healing process.
YWCA programs are voluntary, allowing people to self-refer to peer support or the safe house.
Tiller knows trust is being built when people are ready to talk about their experience.
“So when people start feeling a little bit more comfortable to open up and have those conversations, that's always a massive sign,” she said.
For Boudreau, the time to have those conversations is now.
She said the danger didn’t pass when she aged out of the care system at 19.
She got caught up in a relationship with a man that moved quickly, before taking a troubling turn.
“I believed it because for so long I wasn't chosen,” she said.
Boudreau said she slowly began to feel she was being pushed to do things she didn't want to do. She even discovered intimate photos of herself had been posted online.
It got to a point where she had to get out.
With the help of friends, she found a new place to live and started to rebuild her self-respect.
“It took a long time for me to love myself again,” she said.
Now, she wants to share her story to help others who grew up in provincial care.
“I want to help people see that we're not leftovers,” she said. “We're not just someone you can just pick up and throw away when you don't want them anymore.”
Canadian Human Trafficking Hotline: 1-833-900-1010 – Available across Canada, 24/7

EDITOR'S NOTE: They are among society's most vulnerable: children who experience traumatic instability and end up in government care. In this series called “Left Behind,” the CBC Atlantic investigative team explores the challenges and outcomes through the eyes of people who lived through this and those trying to help them.
