articles.title: Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?
articles.summary: Capt Smit Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard the Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv.
articles.byline: Henry Moore, Sharanya Hrishikesh & Meryl Sebastian

blocks.text: Capt Machchhar grew up in the Indian city of Mumbai, where his parents still live. In 2008, he joined Mainland Air, an aviation college in New Zealand's Dunedin, before joining Indian airline SpiceJet as a commercial pilot three years later. He moved to Dubai and joined Flydubai in 2022, having become an experienced pilot.
Speaking to the BBC, Philip Kean, the CEO of Mainland Air, said he remembers Capt Machchhar as a man who would remain calm in a crisis.
"We trained him for forced landing - not this kind of situation, which is very, very rare," Kean said. "It was a long time back but he came across as a good and honest worker."
Capt Machchhar has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.
His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives".
Last year, Capt Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter.

Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work with his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]," he added.

Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family.
"Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised.
He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely.
"In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations.

At the time of the conversation, Capt Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had had to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues causing delays.
He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want."
Indian social media has been awash with praise for Capt Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral.
Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time) en route to Ben Gurion Airport in Israel.
The flight was carrying at least 150 people, with Netanyahu saying "almost all" passengers were Israeli.

Data from flight tracking website Flightradar24 shows the plane made a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia around two and a half hours after take-off, dropping more than 17,000ft (5,000m) in less than two minutes at around 05:21.
Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code, which indicates a hijacking.
At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.
Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.
Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.
But speaking on Wednesday after the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.

He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".
The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in north-western Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.
The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Capt Machchhar.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Machchhar "showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others" despite being seriously injured.
"His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," he wrote in a post on X, adding that he hoped for the pilot's speedy recovery.
Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar praised the pilot's "extraordinary courage and remarkable presence of mind, even in the face of grave danger".
Speaking to reporters at the White House, US President Donald Trump said that "the pilot was in very bad shape" but had the sense to open the cockpit door during the attack.
"Amazing, in a way he was a hero, to open the door. He was able to fall back and get the door open."

articles.title: ‘Politics can be brutal’: Sarah Hanson-Young speaks out about divisions within Greens
articles.summary:
Greens sources say the relationship between new leader David Shoebridge and runner-up Mehreen Faruqi is seriously strained

  • Get our

blocks.text: Sarah Hanson-Young has spoken out about major divisions in the Greens party room, offering support to newly elected leader David Shoebridge and describing politics as “brutal”.
The South Australian senator contested Wednesday’s leadership ballot, finishing behind Shoebridge and outgoing deputy leader, Mehreen Faruqi.
Former leader Larissa Waters shocked colleagues by resigning on Monday, over serious health concerns.
Hanson-Young was eliminated after the first ballot with only two votes.
“God, politics can be brutal,” she said in a video posted to social media, after a bush walk with her husband on Thursday.
“Friendships made and lost, but it takes all types. We all care so deeply about the future of this country and the future of the planet.”
Hanson-Young said it would take a huge effort to defeat One Nation and its leader, Pauline Hanson, and warned “the radical right” would wreck the country if it wins power.
“Australians deserve a optimistic, caring, and defiant progressive force, and I won’t be backing down,” she said.
“I’m sorry we couldn’t pull it off this time, but buckle up, because we’ve got a lot of work to do.”
Her comments come a day after Faruqi criticised her colleagues for electing Shoebridge and demanded the party’s rank-and-file members be given a say in future leadership elections.
Greens sources say Shoebridge and Faruqi’s working relationship is seriously strained.

The New South Wales senator said she planned to pursue bold politics and radical action to fight “against genocide, wars, surging fascism” and climate change, working from outside “the constraints of the leadership team”.

In an interview with Guardian Australia’s Australian Politics podcast on Thursday, Shoebridge said he and the newly elected deputy, Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May, had received a strong endorsement from their colleagues.
Shoebridge said he could work with Faruqi, praising her for effective community engagement.

“I have huge respect for Mehreen and the work that she does. And, acknowledging as well, the attacks that she gets and the way she keeps turning up proudly and strongly, taking the case forward in the face of all of those attacks.
“That is something that I have immense respect for and gratitude for.”
Shoebridge said Greens MPs wanted Faruqi to continue her engagement with voters and Greens members.
“Sometimes you want to be part of the leadership team. Sometimes you want to be out connecting with the community in a different way.
“We’re all human beings and we all know how in the moment how we can best contribute to the project.

“I take Maureen at her word that that’s how she thinks she can best connect with the community, how she can best connect with the project. And she has my 100% support to go on being the amazing Greens senator that we’ve all seen.”
He committed to giving rank and file party members the right to vote in leadership elections in time for the next scheduled contest, due to take place immediately after the next federal election.
A party plebiscite in 2020 saw 62% of Greens members support a party-wide vote for leader, but the move fell short of a required two-thirds majority.

articles.title: Cristiano Ronaldo walks out of Portugal camp
articles.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo has left Portugal’s camp after learning that he would not start the next Nations League match. Portugal's coach has denied reports of a rift between himself and the star player.

image.caption: Cristiano Ronaldo has seen limited action for Portugal during this international breakImage: Grzegorz Wajda/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The 41-year-old forward left the Portugal camp on Wednesday after coach Jorge Jesus had told reporters at the Matchday-1 press conference that Cristiano Ronaldo would not feature in the starting lineup against Denmark in the Nations League.
The move comes amid reports of a rift between the Al-Nassr player and coach, something that Jesus denied.
The 72-year-old coach conceded that his captain had been disappointed to remain on the bench in Portugal's win over Norway on Sunday, but he insisted that there had been "no incident whatsoever."
Ronaldo didn't explain why he had taken the decision, but in an Instagram post he said that "in time" he would "tell the Portuguese people the truth about the reasons" behind his departure.

"Following the national team coach's news conference, and after a conversation with the president of the Portuguese football federation, I decided to leave the national team's training camp," he said, adding that he had always "dedicated" himself to the national team.
"Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates, without exception."

For its part, the Portuguese federation (FPF) confirmed that the five-time Ballon d'Or winner had left the camp and that the team's preparations for Thursday's match in Copenhagen would continue without him.
"The entire delegation remains fully focused on the national team's upcoming fixtures and on achieving our goals," it said.
It wasn't immediately clear whether Ronaldo's departure would extend beyond the current international break.

blocks.caption: Portugal coach Jorge Jesus has denied reports of a rift between himself and Cristiano RonaldoImage: Kristian Tuxen Ladegaard Berg/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Wednesday's press conference, Jesus had said that Ronaldo would start on the bench and may be brought on as a sub.
"I don't know what's going to happen in the game," the coach said.
"If we need him to play, he'll play. If not, he won't."
Limited action

Ronaldo started Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales last Thursday but was substituted in the 67th minute. He was on the bench but saw no action in Sunday's 2-1 win over Norway in Oslo. Portugal face Norway again at home this coming Sunday.
Portugal leads Group A4 of the Nations League with six points from two matches, three points more than Denmark and Norway.

Wednesday's news comes with Ronaldo's long-time rival Lionel Messi set to play his last match for Argentina next week. Earlier this year, Ronaldo, who is the all-time top goal scorer in men's competitive matches (979), had said recently that this Saudi Pro League season is likely to be the last of his professional career.
Earlier this year, he had said the 2026 World Cup would be the last of his career but did not say exactly when he would retire from international football.

articles.title: Former soldier exposes how Canadian white supremacist group recruits members
articles.byline: Eric Szeto, Jordan Pearson, Christian Paas-Lang, Ivan Angelovski

image.caption: Second Sons Canada requires prospective members to sign a non-disclosure agreement before they can join, according to a former soldier who attempted to join the group before learning its true nature. (Second Sons Canada/Telegram, CBC)

blocks.text: Second Sons Canada describes itself as a "men's nationalist club" dedicated to fitness and preserving Canada's heritage, but a former military member who attempted to join the group says he only learned about its true nature — which includes adoration for Hitler, neo-Nazis and hatred for Jews — when he met them in person.

Not only was the prospective member told to sign a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) that would ban him from revealing confidential information about the group, the recruit said he was also searched for recording devices and asked to say racial slurs as a test.

"They advertise themselves as one thing," said the former CAF member, who CBC News is not naming due to concerns for his personal safety and legal retribution. "And then as soon as I met them … the sheets were pulled down and it was a whole other thing that was disgusting."
He said much of the in-person meeting was about how Jewish people were evil and how Hitler's philosophy was "genius."

"They really, really wanted to know my knowledge of their version of racial ideology history and how it influences today's society," he said. "It seems like they really want to brainwash their new candidates into hatred. And that really put me off."
The former CAF member's account is the first glimpse CBC has gotten into the inner workings of the Second Sons in-person recruitment process.

Previous reporting by CBC's visual investigations team aligns with the source's information. The group itself maintains a carefully-curated image on its official social media platforms. Its leaders, meanwhile, have praised Hitler and the Nazi party, said they welcome neo-Nazis into their ranks and called for mass deportations at gunpoint and the execution of Canadian politicians while talking on personal podcasts and livestreams.

items: 'The Nazis were right': What the leaders of Canada's biggest 'nationalist' group really want

blocks.text: "The organization is clearly anxious about individuals coming forward, speaking to the press or others about their activities," said Richard Moon, Law Foundation Chair at the College of Law, University of Saskatchewan focusing on freedom of expression.

"I think there's a real risk that an NDA like this might have a chilling effect on someone's speech, and particularly on their speaking to the media or the legal authorities about activity they may be concerned about as unlawful."
Since forming in 2024, Second Sons has expanded rapidly. There are chapters across the country.

The group is part of what's known as the "active club" movement, a decentralized assortment of male-focused groups promoting white supremacist ideals. The movement has grown globally in recent years, increasingly moving from online forums to real-world training groups and anti-immigration protests.
Second Sons even folded Quebec-based Frontenac AC — one of Canada's most prominent active clubs — into their group.
Earlier this year, a government report said the active club movement posed a risk of "extreme violence."

items: 'Active clubs' are all over Canada. What are they?
'We will not be intimidated,' Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc chief says of white nationalist gathering

blocks.text: Over the weekend, Second Sons held a demonstration at Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc reserve near a former residential school, also appearing on a Kamloops overpass with a banner that read "Got bones?" The demonstration was condemned by community members and Prime Minister Mark Carney.

"The cowardly act that took place at Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc yesterday, is abhorrent. It has no place in this country. My thoughts are with everyone who are shaken and hurt by this disgusting display of hate," Carney wrote in an X post Monday.
The RCMP say they are taking the matter seriously and "will continue to engage the group as part of our response and current ongoing investigation."

On Tuesday, Second Sons president Jeremy MacKenzie reshared a doctored image to Telegram showing Second Sons members holding the "Got bones?" banner in front of the Auschwitz death camp, where the Nazis killed nearly one million Jews.
White supremacist 'media organization'
The non-disclosure agreement says Second Sons is federally registered as a numbered company: 16130623 Canada Inc.
Corporate documents found in the federal registry of businesses list Jeremy MacKenzie as director, along with Alex Vriend and Alex Cabana as shareholders.

MacKenzie is an Afghan war veteran and the founder and president of Second Sons and its predecessor, Diagolon. RCMP have described Diagolon as an "extremist, militia-like organization." Vriend is a long-time associate of MacKenzie and the vice-president of Second Sons.

Cabana has not been as openly associated with Second Sons as MacKenzie and Vriend. He is an Afghan war veteran who was affiliated with Veterans 4 Freedom, an advocacy group that was formed by central figures in the self-described "freedom convoy" protests that overtook downtown Ottawa in the winter of 2022.
It's not clear how much revenue the corporation has generated because required annual financial filings for the company in 2025 and 2026 are listed as "overdue."

The Second Sons website notes that people trying to join the group must pay an application fee, with a $20 monthly commitment if they are accepted. In livestreams on the video-sharing platform Rumble, Vriend has claimed that the group's leadership don't get paid themselves and rely on income from subscriptions by fans.
A post in the Second Sons public Telegram channel says they are working to set up a "support shop" for the group.

items: Canadian, U.S. fascist fight clubs joining forces south of the border, CBC investigation finds
A white nationalist group visiting Canadian locations is trying to normalize extremism, says a former neo-Nazi

blocks.text: But experts say there are questions about whether the company, which describes itself in the NDA as a "media organization that creates, develops and publishes content," should be allowed to operate due to the nature of its activities.

"Calling for the execution of a politician is not a legitimate activity of any company, let alone a media company," said Richard LeBlanc, professor of governance, law and ethics at York University, who reviewed the documents that CBC located.

The leaders of Second Sons appear to be aware of the rules that a registered company must follow — for example, human rights laws that ban discrimination based on race — and how the organization skirts them.

Addressing a viewer question about the group's admission process in a September 2025 livestream, Vriend said, "Second Sons is an officially-registered organization … I can't speak to what Second Sons' policy is, but in Canada, it is illegal to discriminate based on immutable characteristics like race, gender, disability, et cetera … Can I make that more clear for you? We are an organization that takes members based on meritocracy. Can you read between the lines?"

LeBlanc says if a company is engaging in overly broad NDAs, hate speech, excessive anonymity or face coverings, "that doesn't insulate the company and the founders and the officers and directors and employees of said company from liability and possibly prosecution."

The company's regulatory compliance practices may lead to its failure before anything else. The Government of Canada's website states that it has sent a notice of intent to dissolve the corporation if it does not file its financial statements "immediately."
'They were very cautious'
The former CAF member said he was looking to belong to a community that espoused patriotic views, so he decided to apply after seeing Second Sons content online.

The Second Sons website states that it welcomes former members of the armed forces, if they can show that they are no longer serving. Recently, the group's training — which initially focused on mixed martial arts sparring — has taken on a more military-style feel, including cot-carrying, army crawls and other drills.

items: Large white supremacist meeting shakes residents of Alberta town
No place for 'hate' or 'divisiveness': Politicians condemn white nationalist group's visit to northern Ontario

blocks.text: The source said he did a virtual interview over messaging app Telegram. Following that, they agreed to set up a meeting in Ontario.

"They had me pull my shirt down to make sure I wasn't wearing a wire," he said. "They had me leave my phone face up on the table to show I wasn't recording them. They were very cautious that I would leave first and not follow them."
He said they also spoke about training in hand-to-hand combat skills to prepare for potential violent situations.
Vriend, the vice-president, has publicly advocated for brutally beating counter-protesters.

Referring to a 2025 incident where a man grabbed a flag from the leader of a "Canada First" demonstration, Vriend said the response should have included the leader spearing the man in the face, cross-checking him and punching and kicking him in the head.
"Is he arrested? Yes. Does he catch a charge? Yes. Is it the end of his life? No. Does that immediately become a symbol of resistance for all Canadians? Yes."
CBC's source said he did not learn the names of the men he met.
Undercover applicant

The application process mirrors what happened when two La Presse journalists, Tristan Peloquin and Vincent Poirier, applied to join Second Sons over the summer, under a false name. The existence of the NDA was first reported by La Presse. CBC obtained it independently.

Shortly after applying, the two La Presse journalists received an email that included 17 questions asking for their name, family history in Canada and political beliefs. From there, they were messaged on Telegram by someone from Second Sons — who turned out to be the former leader of Frontenac Active Club, Shawn Beauvais-MacDonald, who has referred to himself online as a Nazi and praised Hitler.
"He was trying to have more information on why we wanted to join Second Sons. And after that, in the first 24 hours, he asked us for a meetup. We were surprised," Poirier told CBC News.

Second Sons also sent a non-disclosure agreement to the journalists, saying that the document "not only legally protects our Organization and its members, it also protects you from having any of the personal information you provide released under penalty of law."
La Presse did not meet in person with Second Sons.
Second Sons did not respond to CBC's request for comment.
Do you have more information on this story? Email us at vi@cbc.ca

articles.title: Overnight, Meta deleted all her accounts. AI customer service won’t let her reach a human
articles.summary: Toronto resident Jasmine Ault says Meta disabled her accounts overnight, without giving her a reason, and that she's been unable to get past their AI chatbots to speak to a human to resolve the…

image.caption: Jasmine Ault, a Toronto resident who used social media for marketing and as a personal scrapbook of her life, says her Meta accounts were deleted overnight, with no reasoning provided to her as to why. When she attempted to appeal, a wall of AI chatbots shut her down, a trend that is being seen acro

blocks.text: When she woke up in the middle of the night last Thursday, Jasmine Ault went to check her phone like she usually would.
But she didn’t expect to see a notification telling her that her Instagram and Facebook account had been permanently disabled by Meta.

It was only the start of an odyssey of frustration and anxiety spanning multiple days as Ault struggled to get to the bottom of how 20 years of personal data and professional contacts had been taken from her overnight — all while being stonewalled by AI customer service with no option to reach a human being, even after paying extra.

“It feels like I've lost everything in a metaphorical fire with my digital albums and my digital memories,” Ault, who lives in Toronto, told CBC News. “And who's going to protect those if I can only speak to AI?”

Ault is only the latest victim in a pattern growing increasingly common over the past two years. Numerous Canadians have reported their Meta accounts being abruptly wiped, leaving them stuck interfacing with AI chatbots unable to grasp the complexities of their situation.

One Canadian lost 18 years of data on Facebook after posting photos from a family trip, and had a second account banned when she tried to return. Others lost accounts vital to advertising their businesses. Many believe their accounts were incorrectly flagged by Meta’s AI moderation, and while some have had accounts restored after reaching out to media, others have never had them restored.
Meta has not responded to a request for comment from CBC News.
It comes at a time when companies are increasingly adopting AI in customer service, despite data showing customers aren’t on board.
Lack of empathy frustrating to customers

A global survey released earlier this year of more than 34,000 customers, service representatives and executives found that half of customers surveyed reported a lack of empathy as their biggest frustration with AI customer service.

And while 87 per cent of customers ranked phone calls as a preferred customer service channel, the survey found only seven per cent of executives plan to prioritize them. The research, commissioned by software company ServiceNow in partnership with research firm ThoughtLab, included 1,350 customers and 195 executives in Canada.

items: AI agents lag far behind human workers. Why are tech companies laying off the humans?
As more teens turn to AI for emotional support, experts say it's no substitute for human connection

blocks.text: Ela Veresiu, associate professor of marketing at the Schulich School of Business at York University, explained that companies are buying into AI en masse despite the backlash because of the promise of efficiency and lower costs.
“It is a lot cheaper to have an AI that responds to customer service queries than to hire people that can potentially respond, or be available to respond, 24/7,” she told CBC News.

But while an AI chatbot is able to direct customers to existing information, such as a business’s hours of operation, they can’t handle complex “why” questions, she said, and it can create huge problems.

If a company has competitors, customers frustrated with poor AI rollout can take their business elsewhere, potentially leading businesses to change strategies. But for singularly massive social media companies like Meta, which offer unique services, there’s no business incentive to change their policies.
“Customers may grumble and be dissatisfied by the overreliance of AI and customer service, but ultimately, they have no choice in the marketplace,” Veresiu explained.
‘It’s people’s lifelines’

Ault started her Facebook account in 2006, the first year it was public. After she received the news that her Instagram, Facebook and even a linked Instagram for her dog had all been deactivated, Ault says she stayed up for the next 26 hours straight, desperately trying to appeal the decision.
Screenshots she shared with CBC News stated that her accounts were disabled because her Facebook “doesn’t follow our rules,” but Ault said she was never told what rules her Facebook allegedly broke.

Ault believes her Facebook had been recently hacked, and that this may have caused her accounts to be flagged. But within minutes of pressing the appeal button, she was told her case was closed and she would not be permitted to appeal again, without giving her the opportunity to plead her case.

She created a backup Instagram account and paid for Meta Verification under the impression that it would allow her to reach a human support agent. Meta’s Verification program has various paid tiers with perks such as enhanced support. Standard, the option Ault went for, costs $14.99 US (roughly $21 Cdn).
But the enhanced support she received was simply another AI chatbot, which swiftly told her the ticket was being closed, and that she had reached her limit of support interactions.

items: Hamilton woman says cooking business erased 'from existence' after Instagram account shut down by Meta
'It's sheer panic': Ottawa restaurateur says Meta wrongly banned her business accounts
Meta suspended his business's social accounts — it took him a month to reach a human

blocks.text: CBC News has reached out to Meta, but the company has not responded to questions about Ault’s account and whether access to a human customer service agent — once a staple of all customer service interactions — is now only accessible at a high monthly cost. Of Meta’s verification tiers, only Premium and Max, which have a monthly fee of $150 US and $500 US respectively, mention the ability to “request a call from an agent.”

“It, to me, feels like Meta is trying to cut corners by not paying a human, when they're worth billions and billions of dollars,” Ault said. “And it feels almost sick to me that they just think, like, 'We can just shut these people's accounts down, they can't get through to us and talk to us,' and it's people's lifelines. It's people's memories. It's people's everything."
She added that since she used social media to provide marketing to clients for her side business, she’s now losing out on those financial opportunities and connections.

Jon Festinger, a lecturer at the Peter A. Allard School of Law at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, said Canadians may have legal recourse to challenge account deletion in court by arguing damages that demand a remedy, particularly if they used their social media for business purposes.
“It should be relatively easy to prove the damages, at least the reputational damage, and perhaps more,” he said.
Local restaurant faces setback after Meta wrongfully shut down their social media accounts

Canadian courts have made some steps toward dealing with AI chatbots — Air Canada was found liable for its chatbot’s hallucinated advice to a customer in 2024, for instance — but there are still gaps in Canadian consumer law when it comes to customer rights and AI, he said.
Regulation needed now, experts say
That’s where experts believe regulation should come in.

"Any technical solution makes mistakes," Shion Guha, an assistant professor at the University of Toronto and director of the Human-Centered Data Science Lab, told CBC News. "What it's really about is that people lack a way to get the mistake fixed."
Companies must be required to provide a clear pathway to a human agent and a fair appeals process, especially if automated systems are being used to moderate social media, he said.

items: Trump says top tech firms have signed accord to 'self-police' AI development
Is AI evolving too fast? A look at the debate on slowing it down

blocks.text: “Literally in every other facet of our life, if we are appealing ... a potentially unfair decision, we reach a human being,” he added, giving the example of speeding tickets and tax appeals.
“People expect that that will transpose to private social media platforms, and it doesn't because … they're not required to, because there's no regulatory framework in place for that.”

An existing model is the EU’s Digital Services Act, which was implemented in 2024 to update rules for online services, including guaranteeing transparency and a full appeal process when content is removed.
Instagram users blame Meta’s AI moderators for wrongful suspensions
New legislation around AI chatbots in Canada was introduced in June, but it focuses on increasing safety requirements to protect children online, not consumer rights.

CBC News has not yet received a response from AI Minister Evan Solomon’s office to questions on whether upcoming legislation will ensure Canadians have the right to access a human customer service agent during appeals processes.

In the meantime, Canadians like Ault have their digital footprints hanging in the balance, hoping that the thousands of photos, conversations and memories lost to their disabled accounts might one day be restored.

articles.title: Tennessee halts woman's execution after 'failed' attempt
articles.summary: Christa Pike was found alive and snoring, despite being administered two injections of a lethal drug. The state governor has ordered a review of the botched execution.

image.caption: Christa Pike was just 18 when convicted of murder in 1995 [FILE: December, 2007]Image: J. Miles Cary/Knoxville News Sentinel/USA TODAY NETWORK/REUTERS

blocks.text: The governor of Tennessee ordered a halt to the execution of Christa Gail Pike, convicted of murdering a schoolmate more than 30 years ago, after authorities "failed" to carry out her execution on Wednesday.
Despite being administered two doses of a lethal drug, Pike was found breathing.
The execution had been scheduled for 11:00 a.m. local time at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution. The injections were administered in front of witnesses, including journalists.
Pike, 50, was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and was taken to a hospital in an ambulance, her attorneys said.
She received treatment at the hospital, but authorities had not yet informed them about her condition, her attorneys added.

blocks.caption: Pike was heard gasping after the injection and taken for medical treatmentImage: George Walker IV/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What do we know about the execution attempt?
Pike would have been the first woman executed in the southern US state of Tennessee in over 200 years.
According to media witnesses, who were observing from a separate room, Pike was strapped to a gurney.
"I'm going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life, and that is in love," she said in her "last" words.
By 8:26 p.m., witnesses reported that the second dose of pentobarbital had been given to Pike.
However, Pike was heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m.
At that time, media witnesses were asked to leave the room.
Tennessee orders investigation into failed execution of Christa Gail Pike
Governor Bill Lee said in a statement that he has ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred" and that scheduled executions will not be carried out this year.

"Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State's most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective," he said.
Pike's attorney filed an emergency motion late Wednesday with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution.
In their appeal, they said she was in "unnecessary agony" and that it was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.
This is the second time an execution has failed in Tennessee this year. In May, Tony Carruthers' execution by lethal injection failed.
Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend committed the murder she was convicted for.
"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done," Pike had said in an earlier statement.

articles.title: Germany news: Merz lauds NATO with Westphalian Peace Prize
articles.summary: At a ceremony to honor NATO, the German chancellor warned that Russia will threaten the rest of Europe if it isn't stopped in Ukraine. In other news, the German military will set up its first drone…

image.caption: NATO chief Mark Rutte was present in Münster to receive the Westphalian Peace PrizeImage: Fabian Strauch/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: October 1, 2026
Merz warns: If Germany falters, Ukraine will too

blocks.caption: Before the award ceremony, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte visited the German-Dutch Corps in MünsterImage: Sem van der Wal/ANP/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a keynote speech on foreign policy, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz issued a stark warning against reducing aid to Ukraine in its defense against Russia.
"If we waver in Germany, then Europe wavers. If Europe wavers, then Ukraine wavers as well," he cautioned at the ceremony in Münster where the Westphalian Peace Prize was awarded to NATO.

Merz specifically warned that Russia could attack Germany and NATO if Ukraine falls. "If we fail to stop Moscow, then sooner or later, the Russian war machine will turn against us, against NATO itself. We must not turn a blind eye to this danger," he stressed.

The German chancellor emphasized that without German aid, the war against Ukraine would result in an "imposed peace." This would lead to mass migration toward the West and the destabilization of the Ukrainian state, according to Merz.
He touched only briefly on the meeting between Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in New York last weekend.

Merz said it was yet another example of how diplomatic efforts fell on deaf ears in Moscow. Russia understands only the “language of strength” and must be brought to the negotiating table through this approach, he stressed.

Merz said "unity and strength remain prerequisites for successful negotiations with Moscow. And this can only encourage us to keep the United States of America by our side in our policy regarding Ukraine".
Merz calls for unity against AfD

Merz said that a united front is also needed in Germany, where the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has seen significant success in recent state elections and currently leads in nationwide polls.

"We in Germany, too, will not allow ourselves to be divided," Merz said. "Not by hybrid attacks, not by social media agitation driven by Moscow-controlled bots, and... not by the slogans of the AfD and its Russian backers."
The AfD wants Berlin to stop providing military and financial support to Ukraine, lift sanctions against Russia, and restore dialogue.
What is Westphalian Peace Prize?
The Westphalian Peace Prize is awarded every two years by the Economic Society for Westphalia and Lippe (WWL).
The award commemorates the Peace of Westphalia of 1648, which was concluded in the town halls of Münster and Osnabrück.
It brought an end to the Thirty Years’ War and is regarded as a contribution to the European peace order among states with equal rights.
This year, NATO was honored for its contribution to the European peace order.

articles.title: K-pop star convicted of violating military service law
articles.summary: The member of K-pop band Winner was given a suspended prison sentence for repeated absences from his national service work.

blocks.text: A South Korean court has handed a suspended one-year prison sentence to K-pop singer Song Min-ho after he was convicted of violating the country's military service law.
The 33-year-old member of the boy band Winner was found to have been absent multiple times at a community centre in Seoul, where he had worked as a social worker from 2023 to 2024.
All able-bodied men in South Korea have to serve at least 18 months in the military. But some are alternatively assigned as social service personnel for health reasons.
The prison sentence handed on Thursday is suspended for two years. That means he can avoid incarceration if he does not commit any crime during that two-year probationary period.
The court heard that Song, who is also known by his stage name Mino, had recorded 102 unauthorised absences during his 21-month stint as a social service agent.
Military service is a duty to be performed "faithfully", and social service agents are "no exception", the court said.
But the court also noted that Song had admitted to the charges and shown remorse.

Authorities launched an investigation into Song shortly after he was discharged in 2024, when local media reported that he was frequently absent from his social service duties and took excessive sick leave.
Song's supervisor at the social service centre was also given a suspended jail sentence for helping him dodge his duties, including falsifying records to make it look like Song had reported to work.
The conscription of South Korea's entertainers has long been a topic of national public debate.

Gangnam Style singer Psy famously had to enlist twice, once in 2003 and another time in 2007, after a Seoul court ruled that he had neglected his duties by continuing his showbiz activities during his first national service stint.

Steve Yoo, one of the country's biggest pop stars in the 1990s and early 2000s, was embroiled in a national scandal after he was found to have evaded military service in 2002. South Korean authorities banned him from the country after he renounced his citizenship and became a US national shortly before he was due to serve in the military.

Going on hiatus to serve in the military is often a threat for budding careers in South Korea's fast-moving entertainment industry. But the evasion of military service also comes with intense public scrutiny and legal repercussions.
Ahead of the ruling on Thursday, Song told reporters that he regretted his actions and was "sorry toward the people who gave me so much love", Seoul Economic Daily reported.
But he did not answer a question about whether he would re-enlist to serve the mandatory duty.

articles.title: Netanyahu says too early to tell who was behind plane incident as flydubai halts all flights to Israel
articles.summary:
Israeli prime minister cautions against early conclusions when asked if there were any signs of Iranian involvement

Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to tell who was ultimately…

blocks.text: Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to tell who was ultimately behind the apparent attempt to crash a ⁠Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight, even as Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations called the incident a “terror attack”, without apportioning blame.

Danny Danon told Fox News on Wednesday night that Israel had “no doubt that it was a terror attack from a radical individual. We still cannot link it to a terror state or terror organisation, but for sure we know there was an intention to bring that plane down.”
Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while the investigation takes place and urged all parties “to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts”.

The incident – which began when one pilot stabbed another on the flight deck in an apparent attempt to take control of the aircraft – is under investigation. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had more than 170 people on board, most of them from Israel.

In what have been hailed as acts of tremendous bravery, several passenger rushed the cockpit of the flight and wrestled the controls from the alleged attacker even as the plane descended sharply, managing to eventually taking control and stabilising the plane before making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, told Fox News host Sean Hannity: “We’ll get to the root of ⁠this attacker, whether he had accomplices” but cautioned that it was “too early to say” when asked whether there was any indication of Iranian involvement.

The pilot accused of carrying out the stabbing was being questioned by Saudi authorities, the Israeli prime minister said, adding that he expected he would soon be taken to the UAE, where the flight took off from. Netanyahu said earlier that he had spoken with the UAE’s president, who agreed that Israel would join the interrogation of the suspect.
Israeli officials, speaking on condition of anonymity to reporters, said the attacker was an Omani national, but there was no comment from Oman or the UAE.

Israel’s foreign ministry later briefed its diplomats around the world that the incident was an “attempted terrorist attack against Israelis, the United Arab Emirates, and the Abraham Accords,” referring to the deal that normalised relations between the two countries in 2020.

But on Wednesday evening Donald Trump told reporters the incident remained unclear, after he had spoken to Netanyahu. “It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack-job, and he stabbed the pilot,” the US president told reporters in the Oval Office.
Netanyahu was among the world leaders celebrating the bravery of the passengers and crew of the flydubai flight on Wednesday.
A video shared by the prime minister’s office showed passenger Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber, speaking to Netanyahu at length about how the events on board played out.

Hayoun told the prime minister how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt the air pressure change as the plane dived before they forced their way into the cockpit and found the attacker at the instrument panel.
“I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during the meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel.
As others wrestled with the attacker, Hayoun said he grabbed the controls and pulled them the way he had seen on television. Then other crew members took over.

The stabbed pilot was identified as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, who was said to have made the emergency call and opened the door to the cockpit, allowing others to rush in and subdue the attacker.

In a post on X early on Thursday, Indian prime minister Narendra Modi lauded Machchhar a “hero”. “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously ‌injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy,” Modi ​said.
Machchhar, an Indian citizen from Mumbai, is being treated in a hospital in Saudi Arabia’s north-western city of Tabuk, where the plane landed safely.

articles.title: Israelis divided as vote that could oust Netanyahu only weeks away
articles.summary:
Some on streets of Jerusalem pledge their support to prime minister while others hope for change

On the streets of Jerusalem, crowded with secular and ultra-Orthodox Jews, religious…
articles.byline: Lorenzo Tondo and Quique Kierszenbaum in Jerusalem; graphics by Ana Lucía González Paz

blocks.text: On the streets of Jerusalem, crowded with secular and ultra-Orthodox Jews, religious nationalists, settlers, Palestinians, and soldiers returning from deployments, uncertainty hangs over an election less than a month away that could mark a turning point for a country profoundly changed after the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023 and nearly three years of war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
The political battle remains on a knife-edge.
For over two years most polls have predicted that the coalition of parties led by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu will collectively slip below the 61-seat threshold needed to form a government.

But there is no clear path to power for his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, even if he maintains current levels of support, because he has ruled out going into coalition with any of the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, who are projected to claim a critical 12 seats.

For Netanyahu to stay in power, he would have to either put together a different coalition or pull off an unprecedented election night surprise. Another deeply fragmented Knesset seems likely, in which neither side is close to securing a majority.

The latest Channel 13 poll, published last week, captured that deadlock: Jewish Israeli parties opposed to Netanyahu were projected to win 52 seats, against 51 for the prime minister’s bloc, with both falling short of the 61 required for a majority.

Eisenkot’s Yashar party topped the poll with 22 seats, while Netanyahu’s Likud was projected to take 18. The lack of clarity over the next government – with both main blocs on the right – is fuelling unease among Israelis, some of whom believe little will change whoever becomes prime minister.

“I’m not going to vote because I don’t trust anyone,” said Rachel, 42, an Israeli citizen living in West Jerusalem. “I used to vote for Yair Lapid,” she added, referring to the leader of the centrist Yesh Atid party. “The party’s name means ‘there is a future’. But today, I don’t see any future for this country.”
Average public trust across the eight Israeli institutions measured consistently by the Israel Democracy Institute, a statistics body, stood at 34% in 2025, compared with 61% in 2012.

An atmosphere of pessimism and indecision is palpable in Jerusalem, where tensions between Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem – the majority of whom cannot vote in Israeli national elections – and rightwing Jewish Israelis have deepened since 7 October. The Hamas attack is likely to weigh heavily on the ballot: a recent poll by the Israel Democracy Institute found that 68% of Jewish respondents said 7 October would be a central factor in deciding how they voted.

“After 7 October, everyone in this government has to take the blame,” said Ilda, who owns a clothing shop on Jaffa Street, one of Jerusalem’s oldest and busiest thoroughfares. Referring to a Haaretz investigation claiming Netanyahu had been warned about the possibility of a major Hamas attack, which he denies, she said: “After journalists exposed what happened, look what they did: they attacked the journalists instead of taking responsibility.”

West Jerusalem has long been considered fertile ground for Netanyahu and the Israeli right. Yet Israel’s growing diplomatic isolation and the prospect of seemingly endless conflict on multiple fronts are beginning to worry voters even here, a few steps from the bustling Mahane Yehuda market, where giant election posters for Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister known for his anti-Palestinian rhetoric and championing a racist death penalty law that in practice applies only to Palestinians, loom over the streets.

blocks.caption: Another advert showing Ben-Gvir at the Machane Yehuda market in Jerusalem.  Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: “This country needs radical change. I think I’ll vote for Naftali Bennett,” said Yosef, 26, a religious Israeli, referring to the rightwing former prime minister who now leads the B’Yachad alliance and is one of Netanyahu’s main political rivals.

On one side are tens of thousands of Netanyahu supporters – called “Bibi-ists” in reference to the prime minister’s nickname – as well as backers of the far-right ministers Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who want to return the current coalition to power to “finish the job” in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon and the West Bank.

On the other are tens of thousands of voters who believe Israel is losing its standing in the world and needs a change of direction – something many see as embodied by the centre-right Eisenkot. His supporters argue that he would place greater emphasis on education, social policy and the economy, areas they say have been neglected by the current government.

“I’ll vote for anyone but the prime minister of 7 October,” said Turgeman as he enjoyed a coffee with his wife at a cafe in Jaffa during the Jewish high holiday season. “I’ve never voted Likud in my life, and I’m certainly not going to start now. I’ll vote for Eisenkot. We need a normal prime minister – someone who also cares about the economy and about prices, which have soared because of the war.”

Food prices in Israel have reached record highs amid the regional conflict and supply chain disruption, with food inflation outpacing the broader consumer price index. The cost of food, including fresh fruit and vegetables, has risen by 9.5% over the past two years.

“They think about wars, while nobody is dealing with the economic crisis,” Turgeman said. “And what has Netanyahu done? He has continued to provide financial support that benefits the Haredi [ultra-Orthodox] community.”

Since 7 October, Israel’s ultra-Orthodox community has been at the centre of a bitter dispute over military conscription. While most Jewish Israelis serve, Haredi men studying in religious seminaries have long been largely exempt.

In 2024, amid war and growing pressure on reservists, the supreme court ruled there was no legal basis to continue the exemption, fuelling anti-draft protests, roadblocks and clashes with police. Haredi parties have blamed Netanyahu for failing to pass legislation to protect the exemption.

Ultra-Orthodox Jews, who make up about 14% of Israel’s population, have traditionally voted for parties backed by their rabbis, including the two main Haredi parties in Netanyahu’s coalition. But anger among younger Haredim over conscription and the policing of protests could lead some to defy their religious leaders this time.

“All the options in this election are junk, but I think I will vote for Eisenkot,” said Pinchas, 24, an ultra-Orthodox student who recently completed his military service. “I have the impression that this time people my age won’t vote according to what the rabbis tell them. Many are angry about the way Netanyahu handled the conscription law, and especially about the crackdown on those who protested against it.”

As the Guardian conducted interviews near Jerusalem’s central bus station, an elderly passerby called out: “There is only one prime minister – Bibi!” It was a reminder that, despite the uncertainty and the opposition’s narrow lead in the polls, the Israeli leader retains a loyal base.

blocks.caption: An advert for Gadi Eisenkot, a retired chief of staff of the Israeli army, on a bus in Jerusalem. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: “I’m sure Netanyahu will win,” said Avraham Levy, 76, a Likud supporter and fruit seller at Mahane Yehuda market. “We’ll have the majority. We need to support Netanyahu because he has to finish the job. If he doesn’t, who will?” he said, referring to Israel’s wars on several fronts.

Among those still backing Netanyahu’s coalition partners are supporters of the far right, including Jakub, 23, who was due to begin his military service soon. “I’ll vote for Moshe Feiglin,” he said, referring to an extreme far-right former Israeli Knesset member who declared in 2025 that the conflict in Gaza was not against Hamas but against every child and baby in the territory, and is now running jointly with the far-right Religious Zionist party. “Because he represents my values, and he has never changed his principles,” Jakub said.

The field is wide open and the divide is also generational: by 2019, support for a Palestinian state stood at about 20%-30% among the youngest Jewish Israeli cohorts, compared with roughly 40%-55% among older generations, reflecting a longer-term shift towards more hawkish attitudes. No more recent comparable data was available.
The difficulty for the anti-Netanyahu camp is that it remains fragmented and has struggled to agree on a coherent political platform or a common strategy capable of uniting its different factions.

Parties representing Palestinian citizens, known as Arab parties inside Israel, could push Eisenkot’s coalition over the 61-seat threshold, but amid a campaign of racism and Islamophobia, he has ruled out going into government with them.
They could potentially support a minority government.

But last week, the Central Elections Committee voted to bar Ra’am and the Joint List, the country’s two main Palestinian parties, from the election, after the far-right Otzma Yehudit party filed a petition arguing that they support terrorism and deny the existence of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state.

The opposition Democrats party filed a similar petition arguing for Otzma Yehudit to be banned for incitement to racism and negating the existence of Israel as a democratic state, because of racist policies pursued in power under its leader Itamar Ben Gvir. That was not upheld.
The decision is being challenged in the supreme court, which has overturned similar bans in past elections.
If allowed to run in the elections, the Arab parties will be crucial to the opposition’s prospects of forming a government and to Eisenkot’s chances of replacing Netanyahu.

Tensions between Palestinian citizens of Israel and the state have deepened since 7 October amid arrests, interrogations and other legal action against Arab citizens, often over protests or social media posts.

blocks.caption: Avraham Levy at his fruit stall in the Mahane Yehuda market. Behind him is an image of Menachem Begin, a co-founder of the Likud party. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: For these reasons, Palestinian citizens of Israel are often reluctant to express their voting preferences. In the 2025 Israeli Democracy Index survey, 70% said they preferred to remain silent about their political views in the presence of strangers, up from 45% in 2016 and compared with 53% of Jewish respondents.

But Palestinian citizens of Israel remain divided over how best to respond, with many pessimistic that any future government will defend rights they say have too often been denied. The Joint List has maintained a more oppositional stance, signalling it could support an anti-Netanyahu minority government from outside while stopping short of joining a coalition, although it has done so in the past.

“These elections are about our strength as an Arab community and our ability to have an influential political voice,” said Amir, 34, from Mashhad in northern Israel, who plans to vote for the Joint List. “We need strong, united Arab representation on equality, discrimination and the Palestinian cause, while cooperating when it benefits our community.”

Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, has instead made political pragmatism its defining strategy. In 2021 it became the first independent Arab party to join an Israeli governing coalition, seeking budgets, services and greater influence for Palestinian citizens of Israel.

“Arab society is being torn apart by crime and violence, while relations with Jewish Israelis are becoming more hostile,” said Abu Mahmoud, 33, from Kafr Kanna, also in the north of the country. “That’s why I’ll vote for Ra’am: negotiate, secure budgets and work with Jewish Israelis where possible.”
He added: “I want politics that can actually improve people’s lives.”
Jamal Risheq contributed to this report

articles.title: New Google Maps images reveal massive scale of devastation in Gaza
articles.summary:
Satellite imagery shows further destruction of homes, businesses and places of worship since fragile ceasefire

An update to Google Maps has revealed the extent of devastation during the…

blocks.text: An update to Google Maps has revealed the extent of devastation during the three-year Gaza war and the severity of the continuing humanitarian crisis faced by the territory’s 2.3 million inhabitants.
The images were taken in June this year and show further destruction of homes, businesses, places of worship and infrastructure since a fragile ceasefire came into effect almost 12 months ago.

blocks.caption: Gaza 2023-2026: al-Mawasi, Rafah

blocks.text: They show huge tented camps lining much of the shoreline, often within a few metres of the sea. Gaza’s once busy main port, now badly damaged and empty of fishing boats, is surrounded by makeshift accommodation. Any available open space in Gaza City is packed with shacks, tents and huts.

blocks.caption: Gaza 2023-2026: Tel al-Sultan, Rafah

blocks.text: The images also show massive damage to northern towns such as Beit Lahiya and Beit Hanoun, as well as the destruction of places of worship such as the Istiqlal mosque in Khan Younis. Major neighbourhoods in Gaza City such as Jabaliya and Shuja’iya, which were targeted in repeated Israeli offensives, are clearly now uninhabitable.

Swaths of rubble are visible in the south of Gaza, where a wide strip appears to have been cleared by Israeli forces along the border with Egypt. The town of Rafah appears to have been almost entirely reduced to rubble and Tel al-Sultan razed to the ground.

blocks.caption: Gaza 2023-2026: Istiqlal Mosque, Khan Younis

blocks.text: More than 2.1 million displaced people are living in tents and temporary shelters in Gaza, where about 82% of structures – roughly 200,000 buildings – have been damaged, with about two-thirds of those destroyed, according to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa.
A recent UN assessment estimated that the number of destroyed structures across Gaza had increased by 9% since the declaration of a ceasefire in October 2025.

blocks.caption: Gaza 2023-2026: Beit Lahiya

blocks.text: “The estimate of the total amount of rubble in Gaza is 61m tonnes. It is approximately 20 times the amount of rubble generated in all wars across the world over the last 18 years,” Jaco Cilliers, the UN Development Programme’s special representative in Palestine told the Guardian last month. The presence of human remains still buried under the rubble remains one of the most urgent humanitarian problems.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the start of the war, mostly civilians. The conflict was triggered by a surprise attack by Hamas into Israel in October 2023, in which militants killed about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and took 251 others hostage.

articles.title: Swiss glaciers lose more than 5% in ice volume in 2026
articles.summary: Over the last five years, Swiss glaciers have lost nearly 20% of their mass, and 2026 saw the second-biggest loss of glacier volume on record. Experts warn there could be no ice left in the next…

image.caption: Scientists have warned of the total loss of the Swiss glaciers in the coming yearsImage: FABRICE COFFRINI/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Glaciers in Switzerland have lost nearly 20% of their mass in five years, experts said Thursday.
The experts said Swiss glaciers are melting rapidly and this year saw the second-biggest drop on record due to unprecedented heat waves in Europe.
There was a drop of 5.5% of Swiss glaciers this year, the Glacier Monitoring in Switzerland (GLAMOS) network found in a new study.
GLAMOS warns of total glacier loss
According to the report, over the past five years, the Swiss glaciers have lost almost ​a fifth of their ice, warning that in the future it could threaten water supplies.
The report also raised questions about the long-term survival of Europe's ice fields.
"Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions," said GLAMOS chief Matthias Huss. "The glaciers this year have lost enormous quantities of ice."
Little winter snowfall and record summer temperatures led Huss to call 2026 "a catastrophic year."
Locals face uncertainty after Swiss Alps glacier collapse
"This is a glacier that isn't surviving," he said. "There will probably be no ice in 10 or maybe 15 years."
The GLAMOS report reiterates concerns about the impact of global warming, especially in Europe, the world's fastest-warming continent.

"The warming that we are experiencing now can be attributed 100% to anthropogenic climate change. It's as simple as that," Huss said, using the term for climate change caused by human activity. "Without human emissions or fossil fuels we wouldn't have any warming at the moment."

articles.title: Japan raises permanent residency fee by 20 times
articles.summary: The hikes are part of immigration policy changes introduced to manage Japan's growing foreign population.

blocks.text: Japan has raised fees for foreigners seeking permanent residency in the country by 20 times to 200,000 yen ($1,270; £955).
Those seeking permanent residency must now also meet new income, pension and Japanese-language requirements.
Long lines formed outside immigration offices earlier this week as applicants sought to beat the fee hikes, with Tokyo's main immigration bureau reporting wait times of over seven hours.
The fee increases are part of a series of changes to Japan's immigration policy under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, which aim to manage its rapidly growing foreign population.

In July, Japan implemented a five-fold increase in visa fees for all foreigners – its first visa fee hike in 50 years. Authorities said this was meant to "reflect inflation and exchange rate fluctuations".
Although immigration remains politically sensitive and restrictive in Japan, the nation's ageing population is increasingly relying on foreign workers to plug a labour shortage.

Japan's foreign resident population surpassed 4.12 million at the end of 2025, marking a record 9.5% increase from the previous year. This however has led to growing anxieties over immigration and social change.
Takaichi has made managing immigration one of her key priorities since she took office in October last year.

In an X post days before the residency permit hikes set in, Takaichi wrote that her government recognises that "some members of the public may feel a sense of concern or unfairness" as Japan's foreign resident population grows.

"To address these concerns, [the government] is working to ensure that its policies toward foreign nationals are orderly, and that both Japanese citizens and foreign residents can live safely and securely," she wrote.
Before the hikes, it would cost non-permanent residents in Japan 6,000 yen each time they applied to change their residency status or extend their period of stay.
From 1 October, the fee varies according to the duration of stay sought – from 10,000 yen for three months or less, to 75,000 yen for five years or more.
Applicants who face financial hardship or are designated as refugees would be granted discounts.
Aspiring permanent residents must now also earn a stable income at or above the Japanese average. Latest data released in July puts average household income at 5.75 million yen as of 2024.
Micaiah Stevens, who has been living and working in Tokyo for 10 years, was not able to compile the necessary documentation to submit his application for permanent residency before the price hike.
The 37-year-old still plans to apply, but questions the new measures aimed at foreign residents.

"My immediate reaction was that foreigners were being treated a bit too conveniently. We're being asked to make more than the average Japanese person, pay a significantly higher fee, just to be able to work in Japan and provide taxes," he tells the BBC.
"There's already a significant language and cultural barrier that prevents some talent from coming over. This just doesn't strike me as a plan that was thought out to the long term."

From April next year, permanent residency applicants will face even tighter requirements, including basic Japanese language proficiency. This has led to a surge in enrollments at Japanese language schools as well as people signing up to take the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, local media reported.

Applicants' expected pension benefits must also be equivalent to that of someone who has enrolled into the employee pension system for 30 years, although the value of one's financial assets can be considered if their expected pension benefits fall short.

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.title: Daredevil Jaan Roose prepares to walk slackline high above central Seoul
articles.summary:
Estonian will navigate narrow ribbon, 160 metres long and 120 metres high, near the city’s famous Gwanghwamun palace on Thursday

Estonian aerial athlete Jaan Roose will attempt to cross a…

blocks.text: Estonian aerial athlete Jaan Roose will attempt to cross a 160-metre long highline suspended 120 metres above central Seoul on Thursday.

Roose, a three-time slackline world champion, will step out on to a narrow polyester ribbon between the Koreana hotel and the Dong-A Media Center, near the capital city’s famous Gwanghwamun palace and square.
The 34-year-old has made a name for himself slacklining dramatic urban environments, such as his 185-metre high feat between Qatar’s Iconic Towers.

In 2024, he became the first person to slackline the strait of Messina between mainland Italy and Sicily, completing the 3.6km traverse despite a fall near the end, caught by his safety harness. Earlier this month, he covered 14.7km over 12 hours on a line above the Danube in Bratislava, Slovakia.

Large crowds in Seoul are expected to watch Roose walk the slackline – twice, at 1pm and 4pm local time – if the weather allows. The walk will be postponed if average wind speeds reach 10m/s or gusts hit 15m/s. Today’s forecast is sunny with light breezes.

blocks.caption: A woman in Warsaw, Poland, watches Estonian slackliner Jaan Roose cross a highline suspended above the city in 2026. Photograph: Marek Antoni Iwańczuk/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Roose said a visit in 2022 to South Korea inspired his Gwanghwamun walk.
On that trip, Roose encountered jultagi, Korea’s traditional tightrope walking, which Unesco added to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2011.
Unlike tightrope walking elsewhere, jultagi is as much comedy as acrobatics. The walker sings, jokes and dances on the rope, trading banter with a clown on the ground as musicians play.

articles.title: California bans child marriage, a practice still legal in 32 US states
articles.summary: Gov Gavin Newsom called it a "long overdue measure to protect young Californians".

blocks.text: Stodden said she would "keep fighting until children are protected from marriage in all 50 states".

She was married to actor Doug Hutchison - known for roles in The Green Mile, A Time to Kill and I Am Sam - in 2011, spurring headlines internationally over the controversy and appearances on several reality programmes in the US, including the VH1 series Couples Therapy.
Other survivors of child marriage also applauded the new law.

"California has sent a clear message to the world today," Brittany Bee, a former child bride, told the BBC. "A message of hope for all children that they may be free from systemic violence. That they may choose their own path."
Bee told the BBC she was wed at the age of 17 to escape an abusive home - only to then be allegedly abused by her adult husband.
"I was just going from one prison to another," she explained. "People have the audacity to tell me that I made a choice - kids, they can't consent."
Bee and other child marriage survivors have been working for years to have child marriages banned in California and across the United States.
About a decade ago, the practice was still allowed across all US state but more and more states have been altering laws. California is the 18th to ban it since 2018.
In the state, there had been no legal age to wed, allowing children to get married as long as their parents consent and a judge signs off on the nuptials.
There was also no mechanism for people under 18 to get divorced and many girls say they were trapped in abusive and predatory relationships.

Unchained At Last, an advocacy group fighting to end child marriage across the US, said about 9,000 girls were wed each year in California and that almost all child marriages involved girls to adult men.
Advocates say that many in the US don't even know that child marriage is legal in so many US states, nor that is has led to allegations of abuse.

Sara Tasneen, who says she was forced to marry a man nearly twice her age when she was 15 years old, told the BBC that it felt "surreal" to finally have the state recognise that child marriage should be banned. She says she started lobbying for this herself in 2017.
She was introduced to her husband the morning of their arranged marriage.
"I was forced to be his wife and that day, my entire life changed," she told the BBC. She became a mother the following year, at the age of 16, and dropped out of school.
"To have seen the arc of this bill come to fruition has been a marathon," Tasneen said. "I'm just grateful that kids cannot get married after January 1, 2027 in California."

articles.title: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies
articles.summary: Scientists say such rapid melting is no longer surprising given the pace of climate change.

blocks.text: Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.
More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".
They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.
The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.
There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.
But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.

The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting.
Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.
"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.
One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.
Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer.

"At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.
Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.
But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear.
"Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion.
"But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."
Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.
Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.
